abstract: The main purposes of this research study are to measure the safety (whether it causes any side effects), tolerability (if it does cause any side effects, how well your body is able to handle them), and reactions, both local at the injection site and systemic, that may occur in the body after receiving VYD2311, or a COVID-19 vaccine, or a combination of VYD2311 and a COVID-19 vaccine in healthy participants. This research study will measure the amount of serum virus neutralizing antibodies produced in the blood (antibodies that block a virus from infecting cells) and pharmacokinetics of VYD2311 compared to a COVID-19 vaccine, when each is administered alone or concurrently. Pharmacokinetics is the study of how a drug moves through the body, including how it is absorbed (taken into the body), distributed (spread throughout the body), metabolized (broken down in the body), and eliminated (removed from the body), and how the body affects the drug.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Neuroinflammation is a characteristic feature of many neurological diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Uncontrolled activation of microglia and astrocytes results in the production of proinflammatory mediators that contribute to neuronal dysfunction and degeneration.
PURPOSE: CRISPR/Cas9 genome-editing technology provides highly precise targeting of genes involved in these pathways, enabling the deletion, correction, or modulation of disease-associated genetic alterations. Nonetheless, effective delivery of CRISPR components to the central nervous system (CNS) remains a major challenge because of protective barriers such as the blood-brain barrier (BBB), as well as concerns regarding genomic instability and immunogenicity.
METHODS: Nanotechnology-guided delivery platforms, such as lipid nanoparticles, liposomes, dendrimers and polymeric carriers, have been developed as promising strategies to address these challenges. These nanosystems can improve biodistribution, pharmacokinetic behavior, and cellular uptake, while potentially reducing off-target effects and systemic toxicity.
RESULTS: The preclinical studies demonstrate successful modulation of key neuroinflammatory targets, including the NLRP3 inflammasome, triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2), Janus kinase (JAK) signaling, and the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway, with potential therapeutic relevance to neurodegenerative diseases. In addition, novel techniques, such as mitochondrial base editing, prime editing, and epigenetic modulation, expand the scope of CRISPR-mediated therapeutic strategies. Although outcomes from animal models are promising, translation to the clinical setting requires careful consideration of safety, ethical concerns, and long-term efficacy.
CONCLUSIONS: This review highlights the potential of integrating CRISPR/Cas9 with nanodelivery systems to advance precision medicine for neuroinflammatory disorders, while emphasizing their potential for therapeutic applications in complex CNS conditions. Ongoing studies aimed at optimizing delivery and reducing off-target effects will be essential for advancing these approaches toward clinical practice.

abstract: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) remains a global health concern due to long treatment durations, limited drug penetration into granulomatous lesions, systemic toxicity, and the persistence of dormant Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The granuloma microenvironment, characterized by hypoxia, acidic pH, enzymatic activity, dense extracellular matrix, and redox imbalance, acts as a barrier to the effectiveness of conventional antitubercular therapy. Recent advances in nanotechnology have led to the development of stimuli-responsive nanocarriers that enable targeted, controlled, and on-demand drug delivery in response to disease-specific stimuli. This narrative review summarizes peer-reviewed literature published between 2015 and 2025 on stimuli-responsive nanocarrier systems for MDR-TB therapy, retrieved from major scientific databases, including PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, Web of Science, and ResearchGate, focusing on granuloma-targeted drug delivery and nanomedicine strategies. Stimuli-responsive liposomes, polymeric nanoparticles, dendrimers, and metallic nanocarriers demonstrate enhanced pulmonary accumulation with improved bacterial targeting and reduced systemic toxicity compared to free drugs. In addition, co-delivery strategies incorporating host-directed immunomodulators further improve bactericidal efficacy. Emerging approaches, including CRISPR-Cas‑based nano-therapies, RNA therapeutics, regenerative and stem cell-based strategies, artificial intelligence‑guided nanocarrier design, and biohybrid delivery systems, represent important future directions. Overall, stimuli-responsive nanocarriers, integrated with next-generation technologies, offer a promising pathway toward precise and effective MDR-TB treatment.

abstract:
PURPOSE: A key pathological hallmark of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is transactive response DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43, encoded by TARDBP) proteinopathy. Mutations in TARDBP and cellular stress can drive nuclear clearance and cytoplasmic aggregation of TDP-43. TDP-43 is an essential nuclear RNA-binding protein that regulates RNA metabolism, and cytoplasmic TDP-43 aggregation leads to aberrant splicing of essential neuronal transcripts including stathmin-2 (STMN2) and unc-13 homolog A (UNC13A). Dysregulated RNA splicing causes cryptic exon (CE) inclusion in STMN2 and UNC13A mRNA, resulting in non-functional proteins and disruption of axonal regeneration and synaptic integrity. Splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides and gene-editing platforms can correct STMN2 and UNC13A mis-splicing defects. However, restoring STMN2 and UNC13A expression alone is not sufficient to regenerate neuromuscular junctions or reverse skeletal muscle atrophy, both of which are crucial for functional recovery in patients with ALS.
METHODS: We reviewed gene-targeted treatment strategies and rehabilitative mechanisms that inhibit ALS progression and reverse neuromuscular degeneration by analyzing databases, including Google Scholar, PubMed, and ScienceDirect. We proposed a dual-modality therapeutic approach integrating base-editing-mediated gene therapy with exercise-based rehabilitation.
RESULTS: Antisense oligonucleotides and genome editing can restore transcript fidelity by preventing cryptic exons inclusion in STMN2 and UNC13A, thereby stabilizing neuronal function. Gene-targeted therapies halt ALS progression; however, these treatments alone are insufficient to reverse neuromuscular degeneration or achieve functional recovery needed for patients with ALS to return to daily life.
CONCLUSION: Integrated rehabilitation is a crucial step in gene-targeted therapy for ALS. This strategy halts disease progression and restores neuromuscular function, thereby improving the lifespan and quality of life of patients with ALS.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains one of the most prevalent malignancies worldwide, with high recurrence rates and chemotherapy resistance posing major clinical challenges. Cancer stem cells (CSCs) are recognized as an important contributors of HCC initiation, metastasis, and recurrence. Within the tumor microenvironment (TME), cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) can maintain CSC properties through intercellular communication. Exosomes serve as essential mediators of this process by delivering long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) from various TME cells (including CAFs, MSCs, macrophages, and HCC cells themselves) to recipient HCC cells.
METHODS: A literature search of PubMed and Web of Science Core Collection (inception to March 2026) was conducted using key terms including "HCC", "CAFs", "MSCs", "Macrophages", "Exosome", "LncRNA", and "Neoplastic Stem Cells". Studies were selected based on topic relevance and methodological rigor; those with incomplete or inaccessible data were excluded. The retrieved literature was synthesized to elucidate the mechanisms by which lncRNAs modulate downstream signaling pathways and to evaluate their translational potential as diagnostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets.
RESULTS: This review identifies multiple mechanisms through which stromal or exosome derived lncRNAs regulate HCC cell stemness, including YAP liquid-liquid phase separation, chromatin remodeling via recruitment of SWI/SNF, INO80, NuRD, and BRM/BRG1 complexes, Wnt/β-catenin pathway modulation through protein stabilization and competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) networks, STAT3 pathway regulation via direct transcriptional repression and transcription factor recruitment, and BMP signaling pathway engagement. Functional classification reveals that these lncRNAs converge on core stemness pathways through complementary transcriptional, posttranscriptional, and protein-level regulatory mechanisms, while integrating signals from the TME.
CONCLUSION: Stromal or exosome derived lncRNAs constitute a critical regulatory layer in HCC stemness maintenance and hold significant promise as noninvasive diagnostic biomarkers via liquid biopsy. Antisense oligonucleotide (ASO)-based therapeutic strategies targeting the stromal cell-lncRNA-CSC axis represent a promising direction. Nevertheless, systematic characterization of stromal or exosome derived lncRNA species, elucidation of lncRNA sorting and uptake mechanisms, and clinical validation of biomarker and therapeutic applications remain important challenges for future investigation.

abstract: Cancer remains a major cause of global mortality, while late-stage diagnosis and therapeutic resistance highlight the need for individualized strategies. Nanotheranostics has emerged as a promising paradigm by integrating cancer diagnosis and treatment within multifunctional nanosystems. However, most current approaches remain technology-driven rather than truly patient-specific. This review examines the emerging convergence of adaptive nanotechnology, artificial intelligence (AI), molecular profiling, and precision medicine to develop intelligent nanoplatforms capable of responding to individual biological characteristics. Based on a literature search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science (January 2010-June 2026), we review nano-enabled diagnostic approaches, including SERS-based nanoprobes and circulating tumor DNA detection, therapeutic strategies such as stimuli-responsive drug delivery, CRISPR-Cas9 nanodelivery, and personalized nanovaccines, and integrated multimodal imaging-guided theranostic systems. We further evaluate clinical trials and translational studies, highlighting biological, manufacturing, regulatory, and ethical barriers to clinical implementation. Although generalized nanoparticle platforms have reached Phase II/III trials and some have received regulatory approval, truly patient-specific nanotheranostic systems remain largely at early clinical stages. AI may bridge patient molecular profiles and nanoplatform design by optimizing nanoparticle properties, predicting biological interactions, and enabling personalized treatment selection. This review provides a roadmap toward adaptive, intelligent, and patient-specific cancer nanotheranostics, supporting a paradigm shift from generalized treatment toward precision-guided personalized healthcare.

title: Nanotheragnosis: an emerging frontier review in personalized cancer medicine.

abstract:
Background:

Warts, hypogammaglobulinemia, infections and myelokathexis syndrome (WHIMs) is a rare disorder that affects the immune system. People with WHIMs can have severe infections all over their body. WHIMs is caused by a mutation in the CXCR4 gene. Treatment with drugs can help control the infections but does not cure the disorder. Researchers want to try a treatment where they collect stem cells from a person with WHIMS, use base-editing to replace the bad gene with a healthy version, and return the new cells to the person. This could cure WHIMs.

Objective:

To test a treatment using base-edited stem cells in people with WHIMs.

Eligibility:

People aged 3 years and older with WHIMs.

Design:

The study has 4 stages.

Stage 1: Screening. Participants will be screened at 1 or more visits. They will have a physical exam with blood tests. A sample of tissue and fluid (biopsy) will be taken from the bone marrow in the hip.

Stage 2: Apheresis. Blood will be taken from the body through a needle; the blood will pass through a machine that separates out the stem cells. The remaining blood will be returned to the body through a different needle. The collected stem cells will undergo gene editing.

Stage 3: Treatment. Participants will stay in the hospital for about 4 weeks. They will receive 3 drugs to prepare their body for the procedure. Then the edited stem cells will be returned to their bloodstream. They will stay in the hospital until they recover.

Stage 4: Follow-up. Participants will have 8 follow-up visits over 5 years. Long-term visits will continue for 15 years.

description:
Study Description:

This is a phase 1/2, non-randomized study of a single infusion of autologous hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells (HSPC) base-edited to repair CXCR4 mutations in 10 participants with (Warts, Hypogammaglobulinemia, Infections, and Myelokathexis) WHIM syndrome.

Primary Objective: Evaluate safety of treatment with BE-HSPC CXCR4 in participants with WHIM syndrome.

Secondary Objectives:

Evaluate:

* Efficacy.
* Genetic correction.
* Immune reconstitution.
* Clinical efficacy.

Exploratory Objective:

Evaluate off-target (OT) editing activity.

Primary Endpoint:

Safety assessed by:

* Incidence of adverse events (AEs) for each participant.
* Evaluate overall incidence of AEs for the study.
* Incidence of serious adverse events (SAEs).

Secondary Endpoints (24 months post-study agent infusion):

* Efficacy: \>= 5% gene edited circulating myeloid cells by 12 months after BE HSPC infusion.
* Gene correction:

  --Frequency of corrected alleles in peripheral blood cells (such as myeloid, T, B, and natural killer \[NK\] cells).

  --\>200/microL edited neutrophils by 12 months post receipt of the BE HSPC infusion.
* Immune reconstitution:

  * T, B, and NK cell number improvement from baseline.
  * B-cell function: immunoglobulin (Ig) production.
* Clinical efficacy: Improvement from baseline problems such as recurrent infection, wart burden, gastrointestinal complaints, or immune dysregulation.

Exploratory Endpoint:

Evaluate for frequency of OTs by high-throughput sequencing (HTS) of the target mutation at the genomic locus 2 years post-infusion.

abstract: Breakthroughs in cancer immunotherapy have been overwhelmingly driven by advances in adaptive immunity, leaving the therapeutic potential of innate immunity largely untapped, a gap in the current treatment paradigm. Trained immunity, defined by the durable, mitotically maintained metabolic and epigenetic memory that innate immune cells acquire after transient stimulation, offers a new approach to addressing this deficit. Here we survey the triggering signals, cellular heterogeneity, and molecular circuitry that govern trained immunity within the tumor microenvironment. We dissect its dualistic character: the mechanistic basis by which trained immunity can either restrain or promote tumor progression, and what this ambivalence means for the design of next-generation immunotherapies. These insights inform a growing pipeline of trained-immunity-based cancer vaccines, which we categorize into four engineered platforms, recombinant BCG, β-glucan nanoformulations, lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-mRNA bifunctional vaccines, and commensal-derived adjuvants. We further propose that vaccine efficacy may depend in part on host immune context, and outline stratification strategies and dosing schedules that may need to be adjusted according to individual immune status, pending clinical validation. In aggregate, evidence from human bladder cancer, preclinical tumor models, and non-tumor trained immunity studies suggests that trained immunity could elevate innate immunity from a supporting role toward an independent therapeutic axis, although most of its direct cancer applications remain at the preclinical or conceptual stage.

abstract:
An open-label, controlled, multi-site, interventional, 2-arm, Phase II/III trial of BNT113 in combination with pembrolizumab vs pembrolizumab monotherapy as first line treatment in patients with unresectable recurrent or metastatic HPV16+ HNSCC expressing programmed cell death ligand-1 (PD-L1) with combined positive score (CPS) ≥1.

This trial has two parts.

Part A, is an initial non-randomized Safety Run-In Phase to confirm the safety and tolerability at the selected dose range level of BNT113 in combination with pembrolizumab.

Part B, is a randomized part to generate pivotal efficacy and safety data of BNT113 in combination with pembrolizumab versus pembrolizumab monotherapy in the first line setting in patients with unresectable recurrent or metastatic HPV16+ HNSCC expressing PD-L1 with CPS ≥1. Patients included in the Safety Run-In Phase of the trial (Part A) will not be randomized to Part B and will continue on-trial treatment (BNT113 plus pembrolizumab) within Part A.

For Part B, an optional pre-screening phase is available for all patients where patients' tumor samples may be submitted for central HPV16 DNA and central PD-L1 expression testing prior to screening into the main trial.

Patients will be treated with BNT113 in combination with pembrolizumab or with pembrolizumab monotherapy for approximately up to 24 months.

abstract: This phase III trial tests how well the addition of dinutuximab to Induction chemotherapy along with standard of care surgical resection of the primary tumor, radiation, stem cell transplantation, and immunotherapy works for treating children with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma. Dinutuximab is a monoclonal antibody that binds to a molecule called GD2, which is found on the surface of neuroblastoma cells, but is not present on many healthy or normal cells in the body. When dinutuximab binds to the neuroblastoma cells, it helps signal the immune system to kill the tumor cells. This helps the cells of the immune system kill the cancer cells, this is a type of immunotherapy. When chemotherapy and immunotherapy are given together, during the same treatment cycle, it is called chemoimmunotherapy. This clinical trial randomly assigns patients to receive either standard chemotherapy and surgery or chemoimmunotherapy (chemotherapy plus dinutuximab) and surgery during Induction therapy. Chemotherapy drugs administered during Induction include, cyclophosphamide, topotecan, cisplatin, etoposide, vincristine, and doxorubicin. These drugs work in different ways to stop the growth of cancer cells, either by killing the cells, by stopping them from dividing or by stopping them from spreading. Upon completion of 5 cycles of Induction therapy, a disease evaluation is completed to determine how well the treatment worked. If the tumor responds to therapy, patients receive a tandem transplantation with stem cell rescue. If the tumor has little improvement or worsens, patients receive chemoimmunotherapy on Extended Induction. During Extended Induction, dinutuximab is given with irinotecan, temozolomide. Patients with a good response to therapy move on to Consolidation therapy, when very high doses of chemotherapy are given at two separate points to kill any remaining cancer cells. Following, transplant, radiation therapy is given to the site where the cancer originated (primary site) and to any other areas that are still active at the end of Induction. The final stage of therapy is Post-Consolidation. During Post-Consolidation, dinutuximab is given with isotretinoin, with the goal of maintaining the response achieved with the previous therapy. Adding dinutuximab to Induction chemotherapy along with standard of care surgical resection of the primary tumor, radiation, stem cell transplantation, and immunotherapy may be better at treating children with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma.
description:
PRIMARY OBJECTIVE:

I. To determine if the event-free survival (EFS) of patients with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma assigned to early chemoimmunotherapy during Induction differs from that of patients who are not assigned to treatment that includes early chemoimmunotherapy.

SECONDARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To determine if early chemoimmunotherapy during Induction therapy improves end of Induction (EOI) response rates and overall survival (OS) for patients with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma.

II. To determine response rates, EFS, and OS following an Extended Induction regimen with chemoimmunotherapy in patients with progressive disease or a poor response to Induction therapy.

III. To compare the toxicities experienced by patients treated with chemoimmunotherapy during Induction versus those experienced by patients treated with standard Induction and to describe toxicities experienced during Extended Induction.

IV. To determine GD2 expression on tumor tissue and tumor cells in bone marrow and assess for associations with response and outcome.

EXPLORATORY OBJECTIVES:

I. To describe the association between tumor and host factors and outcomes in patients receiving protocol therapy.

II. To evaluate circulating biomarkers and markers of minimal residual disease at baseline and during therapy, and assess for associations with response and outcome.

III. To compare patterns of failure between patients treated with and without dinutuximab during induction.

IV. To determine the effect of telomere maintenance mechanisms on end of Induction response rates, EFS, and OS.

V. To explore the impact of high-risk neuroblastoma (HRNBL) and its therapy, including the addition of dinutuximab to Induction chemotherapy, on functional and quality of life outcomes in patients with HRNBL, as measured by caregiver (parent/legal guardian) and patient questionnaires.

VI. To describe the adequacy of diagnostic biopsy specimens, including those obtained by percutaneous core needle biopsy.

VII. To explore the associations between family-reported adverse social determinants of health and both clinical outcomes and biology.

VIII. To develop and validate deep learning predictors of Induction response based on diagnostic MIBG scans. (Imaging Objective) IX. To compare institutional versus central determination of overall response, individual response components (primary tumor, soft tissue and bone metastatic disease, and bone marrow metastatic disease), and poor end of induction response (PEIR) and good end of induction response (GEIR) determination. (Imaging Objective) X. To describe late toxicities (including impaired organ function, neuropsychiatric toxicity, and incidence of secondary malignancy) in patients treated with dinutuximab during Induction or Extended Induction to late toxicities in patients who have not received dinutuximab during these phases of therapy.

XI. To evaluate whether reduced dose radiotherapy to the primary site clinical target volume (CTV) in patients with complete response of the primary site at EOI results in comparable local control relative to historical cohorts.

XII. To compare post-transplant complications between treatment arms, and assess for associations with outcome.

XIII. To assess for associations between EOI response (including good end of Induction response \[GEIR\] and poor end of Induction response \[PEIR\]) and individual response components (primary tumor, soft tissue and bone metastatic disease, and bone marrow metastatic disease) with outcome (EFS and OS).

XIV. To describe and compare the changes in image-defined risk factors (IDRFs) between patients treated with and without dinutuximab during Induction and associate with surgical outcomes and local failure rates following primary tumor resection.

XV. To bank serial samples of blood, bone marrow, and tumor tissue for future research.

OUTLINE: Patients receive Induction cycle 1 and are then randomized to 1 of 2 treatment arms.

INDUCTION CYCLE 1: Patients receive cyclophosphamide intravenously (IV) over 30 minutes and topotecan IV over 30 minutes on days 1-5 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity.

ARM A:

INDUCTION CYCLES 2-5: Patients receive cyclophosphamide IV over 30 minutes and topotecan IV over 30 minutes on days 1-5 of cycle 2 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Patients then undergo stem cell harvest via apheresis. Patients then receive cisplatin IV over 4 hours and etoposide IV over 2 hours on days 1-3 of cycles 3 and 5, and vincristine IV on day 1, doxorubicin IV over 15 minutes, and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days 1-2 of cycle 4 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Patients undergo primary tumor resection after Induction cycle 4 or 5. Following Induction cycle 5, patients undergo testing to determine response to Induction therapy. Patients with a good tumor response proceed to Consolidation, while patients with a poor tumor response proceed to Extended Induction.

EXTENDED INDUCTION: Patients with a poor tumor response or progression during Induction receive temozolomide orally (PO), via nasogastric tube (NG), or via gastric tube (G-tube) on days 1-5, irinotecan IV over 90 minutes on days 1-5, and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours. Treatment repeats every 21 days for up to a maximum of 6 cycles in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. If at any time during Extended Induction testing shows a good tumor response, patients proceed to Consolidation. If after 6 cycles of Extended Induction or if at any time progression is noted, patients are removed from the study.

CONSOLIDATION: Patients undergo two autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantations (HSCTs) during Consolidation. Patients receive thiotepa IV over 2 hours on days -7 to -5 and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days -5 to -2 during HSCT 1. Patients then receive stem cell infusion IV on day 0. Between 6 and 10 weeks after stem cell infusion, patients receive melphalan IV over 30 minutes on days -7 to -5, etoposide IV over 24 hours on days -7 to -4, and carboplatin over 24 hours on days -7 to -4 during HSCT 2. Patients receive stem cell infusion IV on day 0. Between day +42 and day +80 after HSCT 2. Patients receive radiation daily for 12 treatments in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity.

POST CONSOLIDATION: Patients receive dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 4-7 and isotretinoin PO twice daily (BID) on days 11-24 of cycles 1-5. Treatment repeats every 28 days for up to 5 cycles in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. Patients then receive isotretinoin PO BID on days 15-28 for 1 additional cycle, cycle 6.

Patients undergo blood and urine sample collection, echocardiogram (ECHO) or multigated acquisition scan (MUGA), bone marrow aspiration and/or biopsy, computed tomography (CT) scan, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), iodine-123 meta-iodobenzylguanidine (I-MIBG) scan and possible fluorodeoxyglucose position emission tomography (FDG-PET) scan throughout the study.

ARM B:

INDUCTION CYCLES 2-5: Patients receive cyclophosphamide IV over 30 minutes, topotecan IV over 30 minutes on days 1-5, and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 2-5 of cycle 2 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Patients then undergo stem cell harvest via apheresis. Patients receive cisplatin IV over 4 hours and etoposide IV over 2 hours on days 1-3 and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 2-5 of cycles 3 and 5, and vincristine IV on day 1, doxorubicin IV over 15 minutes, and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days 1-2, and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 2-5 of cycle 4 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Patients undergo primary tumor resection after Induction cycle 4 or 5. Following Induction cycle 5, patients undergo testing to determine response to Induction therapy. Patients with a good tumor response proceed to Consolidation, while patients with a poor tumor response proceed to Extended Induction.

EXTENDED INDUCTION: Patients with a poor tumor response or progression during Induction receive temozolomide PO, via NG tube, or via G-tube on days 1-5, irinotecan IV over 90 minutes on days 1-5, and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours. Treatment repeats every 21 days for up to a maximum of 6 cycles in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. If at any time during Extended Induction testing shows a good tumor response, patients proceed to Consolidation. If after 6 cycles of Extended Induction or if at any time progression is noted, patients are removed from the study.

CONSOLIDATION: Patients undergo two autologous HSCTs during Consolidation. Patients receive thiotepa IV over 2 hours on days -7 to -5 and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days -5 to -2 during HSCT 1. Patients then receive stem cell infusion IV on day 0. Between 6 and 10 weeks after stem cell infusion patients receive melphalan IV over 30 minutes on days -7 to -5, etoposide IV over 24 hours on days -7 to -4, and carboplatin over 24 hours on days -7 to -4 during HSCT 2. Patients receive stem cell infusion IV on day 0. Between day +42 and day +80 after HSCT 2, patients receive radiation daily for 12 treatments in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity.

POST CONSOLIDATION: Patients receive dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 4-7 and isotretinoin PO BID on days 11-24 of cycles 1-5. Treatment repeats every 28 days for up to 5 cycles in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. Patients then receive isotretinoin PO BID on days 15-28 for 1 additional cycle, cycle 6.

Patients undergo blood and urine sample collection, ECHO or MUGA, bone marrow aspiration and/or biopsy, CT scan, MRI, I-MIBG scan and possible FDG-PET scan throughout the study.

After completion of study treatment, patients are followed up at 3, 6, 9,12, 15, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 54, and 60 months and then periodically for up to 10 years from enrollment.

trial.official_title: A Phase 3 Study of Dinutuximab Added to Intensive Multimodal Therapy for Children With Newly Diagnosed High-Risk Neuroblastoma

outcomes.description: EFS time is calculated from time of randomization to Arms A or B to first episode of disease relapse or progression, second malignancy, or death, or until last contact if no event has occurred.
outcomes.measure: Event free survival (EFS)

outcomes.description: The response rate will be calculated among all evaluable patients at end of Induction. Responders are defined as patients who achieve a \>= partial response per the revised 2017 International Neuroblastoma Response Criteria (INRC)
outcomes.measure: End of Induction (EOI) response rate
outcomes.time_frame: From randomization to end of extended Induction, up to 12 months

outcomes.description: OS time is calculated from time of randomization to Arms A or B until death, or until last contact if patient is alive.
outcomes.measure: Overall survival (OS)

outcomes.description: The proportion of patients with at least one grade 3 or higher non-hematologic toxicity or grade 4 or higher hematologic toxicity during protocol therapy, graded according to the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0, will be reported.
outcomes.measure: Incidence of adverse events

outcomes.description: Dinutuximab binding to pre-therapy patient tumor samples will be measured and categorized as high or low.
outcomes.measure: GD2 expression

outcomes.description: A series of univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards (for EFS and OS) and logistic regression (for responders vs. non-responders) models will be fit for patients in Arms A and B to evaluate the relationship between tumor and host factors (including tumor ALK and other somatic mutations, copy-number aberrations, gene fusions, gene expression, and pathogenic germline variants) and chemo-immunotherapy during Induction with outcome.
outcomes.measure: Association between tumor and host factors and outcomes

outcomes.description: Will be assessed by comparing the proportion of patients with detectable vs. non-detectable tumor markers (including circulating tumor deoxyribonucleic acid, circulating free DNA, circulating tumor cells, and immune function profiling) between Arms A and B during and after induction and post-consolidation therapy using chi-squared tests at each individual time point, and Cochran's Q across time points to determine if there is a consistent difference in proportions between arms across time. In addition, the tumor markers will be analyzed as continuous variables using longitudinal data analysis methodology such as mixed effects models or generalized estimating equations as appropriate.
outcomes.measure: Circulating biomarkers and markers of minimal residual disease

outcomes.description: The impact of early or late chemoimmunotherapy during Induction on the probability of the involvement of a specific disease site at first relapse will be evaluated using Fisher's exact test.
outcomes.measure: Patterns of failure

outcomes.description: A series of univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards (for EFS and OS) and logistic regression (for responders vs. non-responders) models will be fit for patients in arms A and B to evaluate the relationship between telomere maintenance mechanism and chemoimmunotherapy during Induction with outcome. Patients will be classified into 3 groups by telomere maintenance mechanism (TMM) based on messenger ribonucleic acid expression of TERT and analysis of telomeric DNA C-circles: telomerase (TERT) positive, alternative of lengthening of telomeres (ALT) positive, or no identified TMM.
outcomes.measure: Effect of telomere maintenance mechanisms

outcomes.description: Will descriptively summarize and compare the total Memorial Symptom Assessment Scale scores, total sub-domain scores, and individual symptom scores between patients randomized to receive dinutuximab during Induction (Arm B) to those of patients randomized to standard Induction (Arm A).
outcomes.measure: Functional and quality of life outcomes
outcomes.time_frame: At serial time points during Induction, Extended Induction, Post-Consolidation, and at the end of therapy

outcomes.description: Will be evaluated by descriptively comparing the successful delineation of histologic classification, MYCN amplification status, and ALK status via the traditional method of obtaining tissue for diagnosis, open surgical biopsy, versus the less invasive percutaneous core needle biopsy.
outcomes.measure: Adequacy of diagnostic biopsy specimens

outcomes.description: Kaplan-Meier curves of EFS and OS will be generated and used to calculate 3-year EFS and OS estimates. Associations between social determinants of health (SDOH) and survival outcomes and time to receipt of dinutuximab will be evaluated with univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazard models. Log-binomial regression will be used to estimate risk ratios and 95% CI for the occurrence of dinutuximab consent to randomization and therapy receipt by SDOH exposure. Effect modification of outcomes as a function of poverty, stratified by race/ethnicity, will be explored.
outcomes.measure: Associations between family-reported adverse social determinants of health and both clinical outcomes and biology

outcomes.description: Scans will be given as input to a convolutional neural network trained to predict EOI response.
outcomes.measure: Develop and validate deep learning predictors of Induction response (imaging objective)
outcomes.time_frame: At diagnosis, EOI, during Extended Induction, and end of Extended Induction

outcomes.description: Will be assessed by calculating the percentage of patients receiving the same EOI institutional and centrally reviewed determination of overall response, individual response components (primary tumor, soft tissue and bone metastatic disease, and bone marrow metastatic disease), and PEIR and GEIR. In addition, Cohen's kappa will be calculated to evaluate the concordance in each of these response measures.
outcomes.measure: Compare institutional versus central determination of overall response, individual response components, and PEIR and GEIR determination (imaging objective)

outcomes.description: Will be addressed by calculating the proportion of treated patients with each late effect, including but not limited to impaired organ function, neuropsychiatric toxicity, and secondary malignancy. A 95% confidence interval will be placed on each proportion.
outcomes.measure: Incidence of late toxicities

outcomes.description: The cumulative incidence of local progression (CILP) in patients with complete response of the primary site at EOI and GEIR on this study will be compared to the CILP rate of 11.2±1.8% observed on ANBL0532 using Gray's test.
outcomes.measure: Reduced dose radiotherapy to the primary site clinical target volume (CTV) in patients with complete response of the primary site at EOI results in comparable local control relative to historical cohorts

outcomes.description: Will be evaluated by calculating the incidence of endothelial injury complications and non-relapse mortality within 100 days of transplant, transplant-associated thrombotic microangiopathy (TA-TMA), severe TA-TMA, and sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS) on Arms A and B and comparing between arms with a chi-squared test. The impact of TA-TMA occurrence on the timing or exclusion of subsequent therapy and interventions utilized to treat the TA-TMA, and associations with outcomes (EFS and OS) will be assessed.
outcomes.measure: Post-transplant complications

outcomes.description: Log-rank tests will be used to explore the association between EOI response (using both the revised INRC and GEIR/PEIR classification) and individual response components (primary tumor, soft tissue and bone metastatic disease, and bone marrow metastatic disease) with outcome (EFS and OS).
outcomes.measure: Associations between end of induction (EOI) response and individual response components

outcomes.description: The proportion of patients in the analytic cohort for whom each particular IDRF and also the presence of any IDRF is absent prior to surgical resection will be computed. McNemar's test for paired observations will be applied to determine whether there is a difference in the proportion of each IDRF and any IDRF present before and after initial therapy, and conditional logistic regression will be used to compare between treatment arms A and B. The IDRF status after initial therapy and whether there has been a change from diagnosis will be associated with surgical outcome (complete vs. incomplete resection, presence or absence of surgical complications) using chi-squared tests, and compared between treatment arms A and B with the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test. The association of IDRF status with presence or absence of local failure after primary tumor resection will also be evaluated using a chi-squared test, and compared between treatment arms A and B with the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel.
outcomes.measure: Changes in image-defined risk factors (IDRF)

abstract: Adeno associated viral (AAV) delivery of CRISPR-Cas9 enables efficient, targeted hepatic gene disruption composed of both small insertions and deletions (INDELs) and larger DNA structural variants (DNA-SVs), which are difficult to quantify. Here, we present a protocol for quantifying AAV-CRISPR-mediated gene editing in mice. We describe guide RNA (gRNA) design, plasmid cloning, delivery of AAV-CRISPR to the liver, and execution of liver DNA-editing analysis. This protocol enables quantification of INDELs and DNA-SVs, allowing for validation of gene disruption. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Chan et al.1.

title: Protocol for quantification of AAV-CRISPR-mediated hepatic gene editing in mice.

abstract: Land plant mitochondria and plastids are endosymbiotic organelles that possess their own, reduced genomes. Gene expression is largely regulated at the transcript level, predominantly by nuclear-encoded proteins. Notably, up to thousands of cytidines in organellar RNAs are specifically edited to uridines, mostly restoring conserved genetic information. Key players in this process are nuclear-encoded pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) proteins, which bind target RNAs in a one-PPR:one-nucleotide manner, following a two-amino-acid-based code. Cytidine deamination is catalyzed by intrinsic or trans-acting DYW domains. The modularity and programmability of PPR-RNA interactions make PPR editing factors attractive candidates for the development of biotechnological tools. However, RNA target selection is not determined by the 'PPR code' alone, hampering the generation of highly effective and specific editors. Refining such tools requires efficient assays to dissect the determinants of editor-RNA interaction. Here, we introduce a rapid assay to assess PPR editor specificity through transient expression in the cytosol of Nicotiana benthamiana, which offers a large and diverse transcriptome that enables extensive off-target editing. Profiling of these off-targets provides comprehensive information on an editor's target selectivity. Compared with a previous setup in the model moss Physcomitrium patens, which relies on stable transformation, the required experimental time is reduced from months to days. We demonstrate the power of the system by characterizing the off-targets of the moss editor PpPPR56. The new assay allows rapid functional assessment of editing factor variants and removes a bottleneck in understanding editor-RNA interactions, which is a prerequisite for the rational improvement of PPR-based RNA editing tools.

abstract: The FUNCtion Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) trial is a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 1/2 trial to evaluate the safety and tolerability of TRCN-1023 in adults living with ALS. TRCN-1023 is an investigational medicine given as a single injection into the fluid surrounding the spine (intrathecal injection). The trial will also assess how the body processes the drug and whether it shows early signs of benefit over 24 weeks.
description: TRCN-1023 is an investigational medicine designed to restore the function of a protein called UNC13A, which becomes disrupted in most people with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) due to a breakdown in how nerve cells process genetic information. This trial is designed to evaluate the safety and tolerability of TRCN-1023 given as a single injection into the fluid surrounding the spine, and to identify the best dose to carry forward into future studies. TRCN-1023 stays in the brain and spinal cord long enough that it may only need to be administered once every 24 weeks. The trial will also assess how the body processes the drug, whether it engages its intended target, and its effects on disease progression, physical function, and quality of life.

abstract: Tumor-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) are emerging as critical mediators of metabolic adaptation, yet their role in orchestrating ferroptosis resistance within the tumor microenvironment remains poorly understood. Here, we show that highly malignant osteosarcoma (OS) cells respond to ferroptotic stress by secreting EVs enriched with Alpha-enolase (ENO1). These EVs-ENO1 not only bolster the antioxidant capacity of tumor cells but also confer widespread ferroptosis resistance to macrophages and neutrophils, fostering an immunosuppressive niche. To disrupt this metabolic defense, we developed an OS-targeting lipid nanoparticle (LNP) system for the synergistic delivery of BAP1 mRNA and ENO1 siRNA. We demonstrate that this dual-delivery platform enhances ferroptosis through two complementary regulatory pathways, BAP1/SLC7A11 and ENO1/GPX4, leading to potent lipid peroxidation and tumor cell death. In syngeneic orthotopic and lung metastasis models, these targeted LNPs significantly suppress tumor progression and catalyze anti-tumor immunity by activating M1-type macrophages and cytotoxic T cells. Our findings identify the secretion of EVs-ENO1 as a key reactive mechanism against ferroptosis and provide a translatable nanomedicine strategy to overcome metabolic and epigenetic resistance in solid tumors.

title: A Dual-Delivery System Designed to Overcome EV-Mediated Ferroptosis Resistance for Efficient Solid Tumor Therapy.

abstract: Neural crest cells, a multipotent vertebrate stem cell population, undergo a tightly regulated epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) to delaminate from the neural tube and initiate migration. Neural crest EMT is controlled by a transient pulse of Draxin, which acts as a molecular rheostat of canonical Wnt signaling, and is then rapidly downregulated by unknown mechanisms. To address this, here we use in vivo reporter assays and live RNA imaging to show that Draxin mRNA is rapidly degraded posttranscriptionally via its 3' untranslated region. We found that Draxin transcripts are targeted to cytoplasmic processing bodies (P-bodies), which are membrane-less sites of RNA processing and decay. Disruption of P-bodies by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated depletion of the RNA helicase DDX6 prevented posttranscriptional downregulation of Draxin and impaired neural crest EMT in vivo. These findings parallel observations in human patients carrying DDX6 mutations, who exhibit defects in P-body assembly and craniofacial abnormalities associated with neural crest dysfunction. Together, our results identify P-bodies as regulators of Draxin mRNA decay and reveal a spatially organized mechanism of RNA turnover that controls neural crest EMT during vertebrate development.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Coronary artery disease (CAD) and prostate cancer share common genetic and epigenetic risk factors. Xeroderma Pigmentosum group F (XPF), a DNA repair endonuclease, has been implicated in genomic stability and epigenetic regulation. This study investigated the association between XPF expression and epigenetic changes during T helper (TH) cell differentiation in CAD-associated prostate cancer (CAD-PC).
RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS: CD4+ T cells isolated from healthy controls and CAD-PC patients were subjected to CRISPR/Cas9-mediated XPF knockout or overexpression. TH cell differentiation, chromatin enrichment, global m6A RNA methylation, DNA methylation, R-loop formation, and tumor cell cytotoxicity were evaluated using molecular and functional assays.
RESULTS: XPF overexpression was associated with increased TH1 differentiation and elevated expression of XPF and TP53, whereas TH2, TH17, and Treg-associated markers were reduced. Increased enrichment of XPF and H3K4me3, together with reduced HDAC1, γH2A.X, and H3K27me3 enrichment, was observed at the TBX21 and IFNG loci. XPF overexpression was also associated with increased global m6A RNA methylation, reduced DNA methylation at TH1-associated loci, decreased R-loop accumulation, and enhanced tumor cell cytotoxicity in vitro.
CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that XPF expression is associated with a TH1-skewed epigenetic and immune profile in CAD-PC. However, the absence of disease-specific comparison groups and in vivo validation limits mechanistic interpretation, and further studies are required to establish causality. The present findings demonstrate an association between XPF and the observed TH1-associated epigenetic changes.

title: Association of Xeroderma Pigmentosum group F (XPF) with epigenetic regulation of T helper cell differentiation in coronary artery disease-associated prostate cancer.

abstract: Parkinson disease is an ongoing neurodegenerative disorder, and both motor and non-motor symptoms are involved with the existing therapies having minimal effects on the disease but only symptom alleviation. The goal of this systematic literature review was to generalize up-to-date evidence on the next-generation pharmacological strategies to manage the symptoms and the disease in a patient with Parkinson disease. The review was based on PRISMA 2020 and included the analysis of peer-reviewed studies of human research published in 2015-2026 and retrieved in the key databases, such as PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library. This included 30 eligible studies consisting of randomized studies, observational studies, and early clinical trials. The results show that, although dopaminergic treatment continues to play a central role in managing motor symptoms, new methods such as gene therapy, gene editing, stem cell-based regeneration, nanomedicine delivery systems, repurposed drugs, artificial intelligence-based precision medicine approaches have a good neuroprotective and disease-modifying potential. Nonetheless, the majority of new interventions are still in preclinical or first line clinical phase, with a defined subset of emerging gene-, cell-, and nanotechnology-based approaches evaluated only in animal or in-vitro models rather than in PD patients and associated with small sample size, invasive delivery, limited follow-up and lack of long-term safety information. In general, the review concludes by stating that there has been significant advancement in diversification of therapeutic targets and mechanisms, but rigorous large-scale biomarker-directed clinical trials are needed to translate these advances to effective and sustainable treatment of the Parkinson disease.

title: Next-generation pharmacological strategies for Parkinson's disease: a systematic literature review of symptom management and disease modification.

abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is a degenerative joint disease primarily driven by the disruption of homeostasis in the chondrocyte extracellular matrix (CECM). This review systematically examines the central role of CECM homeostasis in KOA pathogenesis and summarizes recent advances in this field. We synthesized contemporary basic and clinical research to analyse the mechanisms underlying CECM homeostatic imbalance. These include biomechanical stress, inflammatory responses, programmed cell death (e.g., apoptosis, pyroptosis, ferroptosis), impaired autophagy, and cellular senescence. We also evaluated intrinsic risk factors and the application of related biomarkers for diagnosis and prognosis. Our analysis identifies multifaceted pathways driving CECM imbalance and highlights promising multi-modal therapeutic strategies. These include novel pharmacological agents (e.g., high-purity chondroitin sulphate, natural active monomers), physical and regenerative therapies (e.g., stem cells, platelet-rich plasma), precision interventions (e.g., gene editing, RNA interference), and tissue engineering approaches (e.g., smart biomaterials, biomimetic scaffolds). The evidence demonstrates that these strategies can effectively modulate CECM metabolism, promote cartilage repair, and slow disease progression. Targeting CECM homeostasis is a core strategy for developing disease-modifying therapies for KOA. Future efforts should focus on interdisciplinary integration, individualized precision medicine, and multi-site synergistic interventions. This review provides a comprehensive foundation for innovating strategies to delay or reverse KOA progression by restoring CECM balance.

title: Cartilage Extracellular Matrix Homeostasis in Knee Osteoarthritis: Pathomechanisms and Therapeutic Targeting.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Nemaline myopathy (NM) is a clinically and genetically heterogeneous disease caused by mutations in sarcomere-associated genes, with congenital forms representing the most severe end of the spectrum. Recessive mutations in KLHL41 underlie a severe congenital NM characterized by sarcomeric disorganization and impaired muscle growth. The in vivo mechanisms by which KLHL41 governs sarcomere assembly and growth remain poorly understood.
METHODS: We generated zebrafish models of KLHL41 deficiency by the CRISPR-Cas9 approach to examine the temporal and molecular basis of sarcomere assembly defects in NM. The phenotypic and physiological characterization of skeletal muscle defects was investigated by birefringence, spontaneous coiling, spontaneous swimming behavior, and force generation assays. Structural analyses by electron microscopy and immunofluorescence assessed myofibril organization and sarcomere structures across developmental time points. Quantitative proteomics and biochemical assays were performed to identify perturbations in sarcomeric proteins and associated molecular pathways.
RESULTS: We show that Klhl41b is essential for the formation and organization of sarcomeres, supporting both radial and longitudinal muscle growth. Loss of Klhl41b resulted in reduced sarcomere size, defective sarcomere assembly followed by progressive destabilization of sarcomeres, nemaline body formation, and reduced muscle function. Proteomic analysis in Klhl41b-deficient zebrafish revealed reduced abundance of the sarcomeric troponin complex proteins, altered abundance of components of the translational machinery, and increased abundance of components of atrophy-associated pathways.
CONCLUSIONS: These data show that Klhl41b is required for sarcomere assembly and growth, and its deficiency drives a cascade of structural and molecular changes underlying skeletal muscle hypotrophy and NM pathology. These findings advance our understanding of disease mechanisms and may inform targeted therapeutic strategies to restore sarcomere integrity and muscle function.

abstract: Non-invasive monitoring of cellular and molecular events is essential for advancing precision medicine. While exogenous probes often suffer from signal dilution, iron-storage protein-based MRI reporter genes offer an alternative for longitudinal tracking, because contrast is regenerated by the cells themselves. Especially ferritin and its engineered variants have attracted growing interest due to their ability to regulate intracellular iron and generate endogenous T2/T2* contrast. This review summarizes the molecular mechanisms and design principles of iron-based MRI reporter genes, and examines recent developments including CRISPR-mediated integration and manganese-dependent "Bright Ferritin" platforms, which generate positive T1 contrast but require repeated administration of exogenous manganese. Preclinical studies have tracked cellular dynamics in vivo and monitored transgene expression after viral gene delivery, although the evidence base remains almost entirely preclinical. Nevertheless, a persistent challenge lies in generating sufficiently strong MRI contrast while maintaining the delicate balance of intracellular iron metabolism on which these reporters depend. By linking molecular design to imaging performance, this review distinguishes what has been demonstrated experimentally from what remains prospective, and identifies the quantitative and safety questions that stand between the current evidence and clinical use.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: β-klotho (KLB), the obligate co-receptor for fibroblast growth factor (FGF) 19 and 21 signalling, has emerged as a therapeutic target for metabolic disease. Current understanding of KLB function is based largely on germline knockout mouse models, where developmental abnormalities obscure its function in adult physiology. Here, we used somatic hepatocyte-specific gene editing in adult mice to define hepatic KLB function.
METHODS: Hepatocyte-specific KLB deficiency was induced by retro-orbital delivery of adeno-associated virus particles containing guide RNAs targeting Klb in adult male mice expressing Cas9 in the liver. Following transduction, mice were maintained on a 4-week chow diet or a 12-week high-fat diet, prior to comprehensive metabolic and biochemical phenotyping.
RESULTS: Adult-onset hepatic KLB deficiency did not alter body weight or composition, indicating that reduced bodyweight in germline models reflects developmental effects. In line with previous studies, KLB deficiency resulted in derepressed bile acid synthesis, elevated faecal bile acid excretion, and a shift towards a more hydrophobic bile acid pool. Importantly, we also uncovered a role for hepatic KLB in regulating lipid homeostasis. Chow-fed KLB-deficient mice exhibited reduced circulating very-low-density lipoprotein levels (VLDL) with marked hepatic triglyceride accumulation, suggesting altered VLDL metabolism as a potential mechanism driving steatosis.
CONCLUSIONS: Using an adult-onset liver-specific knockout model, we disentangled KLB function from developmental confounders and established KLB as a critical regulator of adult lipid and lipoprotein homeostasis. Our study redefines the physiological role of KLB in hepatic metabolism and has important implications for the interpretation of FGF19/KLB-directed therapies for metabolic diseases.

title: Adult-onset deficiency of β-klotho in the liver reveals a novel role in lipid homeostasis.

abstract: Oncogenic RAS pathway mutations are associated with therapeutic resistance in acute myeloid leukemia, and identification of therapeutic vulnerabilities has been hindered by a lack of clinically relevant models and tractable ex vivo platforms. We utilize a bone marrow endothelial cell co-culture system to perform CRISPR screens on wild-type hematopoietic cells and isogenic leukemias with and without mutant Nras. We credentialed Elovl1, a very long chain fatty acid elongase, as a dependency in RAS pathway mutant leukemia using genetic and pharmacologic approaches. Metabolic and genetic studies in primary leukemias revealed that the fitness defect from Elovl1 loss reflects a mutant-specific dependency on de novo sphingolipid biosynthesis, specifically sphingomyelin production, as Sgms1 deletion phenocopies Elovl1 loss. Sphingomyelin-mediated generation of lipid rafts, key scaffolds for multiple signaling pathways, is essential to the survival of Nras-mutant AML cells. Our work leverages a new leukemia model to identify a targetable dependency in this treatment-refractory leukemia.

abstract: The localized delivery of RNA therapeutics to mineralized tissue interfaces is limited by poor retention and rapid clearance at the target site. We report the development of a solid-phase transfection platform that functionalizes mineralized surfaces into bioactive nucleic acid reservoirs. Through the rational design and screening of a library of 21 piperazine-linked bisphosphonate ionizable lipids, we identified a lead formulation of bisphosphonate lipid nanoparticle (BP-LNP) that maximizes hydroxyapatite affinity without compromising transfection potency. Upon adsorption onto mineral substrates, these BP-LNPs resisted fluid removal and maintained surface-mediated, sustained delivery of encapsulated RNA cargo to adjacent cells. We demonstrated the versatility of this Mineralized Tissue-Targeting Expression System (MiTEX) composed of BP-LNPs in two therapeutic contexts: Cre recombinase mRNA-functionalized allogeneic bone grafts to genetically label de novo bone formation in vivo, and STAT3 siRNA delivery to reduce inflammation in human gingival explants. This platform provides a universal strategy for transforming inert calcium phosphate materials and tissues into locally bioactive RNA delivery systems for regenerative and immunomodulatory applications.

title: Chemically tailored lipids mediate solid-phase RNA programming of mineralized microenvironments.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) remains a leading cause of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma worldwide, but long-term or even lifelong viral suppression with nucleos(t)ide analogues (NAs) seldom clears hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), so-called 'functional cure.' In recent years, a shift in treatment strategy from viral suppression toward cure has emerged, catalyzed by three revised international hepatitis B guidelines (2025-2026) and the first-in-class phase 3 evidence that a finite antiviral therapy, the antisense oligonucleotide bepirovirsen, can achieve a functional cure in about one in five NA-suppressed CHB patients with baseline HBsAg below 3000 IU/mL.
AREAS COVERED: We evaluated the spectrum of established and emerging treatment options for CHB, organized around quantitative HBsAg (qHBsAg) as the axis for selecting and sequencing therapy. Coverage spans backbone NAs and pegylated interferon-α, an HBsAg-guided roadmap, finite NA therapy and off-treatment outcomes, bepirovirsen, other virus-targeting and immunomodulatory agents, and genome-directed covalently closed circular DNA silencing and editing.
EXPERT OPINION: Bepirovirsen's approaching approval is an inflection point. qHBsAg should guide personalized, sequential therapy, with partial cure (HBsAg < 100 IU/mL) as a potential intermediate target when functional cure is unlikely. Durability, standardized biomarkers, rational combination design, metabolic co-management and equitable access are the priorities; a sterilizing cure remains distant.

title: Evaluating the potential of treatment options for chronic hepatitis B.

abstract: The recent spread of clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 high pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI) viruses into mammals, despite limited human infections to date, has raised serious public health concerns and highlights the need for rapidly deployable vaccines, such as mRNA-based platforms, to strengthen pandemic preparedness. Here, we evaluated the effectiveness of an mRNA vaccine encoding the HA of NIID-002, a WHO-recommended H5 candidate vaccine virus (CVV) derived from A/Ezo red fox/Hokkaido/1/2022 (clade 2.3.4.4b) against A/Texas/37/2024 (TX37; clade 2.3.4.4b) and A/Cambodia/2311257/2023 (Cam23; clade 2.3.2.1e). The mRNA was formulated with ssPalmO, a low-inflammatory self-degradable ionizable lipid nanoparticle (LNP). BALB/c mice were immunized intramuscularly twice with the mRNA-LNP vaccine containing either 1 μg or 10 μg of H5 HA mRNA. After boosting, strong, dose-dependent serum IgG responses against NIID-002 HA were detected by ELISA. The mice were then challenged with a lethal dose of homologous TX37 or heterologous Cam23. All mice in the 10-μg group survived both challenges, demonstrating robust cross-clade protection. In the 1-μg group, complete protection without significant body weight loss was observed against TX37, whereas partial protection was observed following Cam23 challenge. Viral titers were significantly reduced in multiple tissues of the vaccinated mice compared to the unvaccinated controls. Our findings demonstrate that the NIID-002-HA mRNA vaccine confers protection against homologous and heterologous zoonotic H5N1 strains in a mouse model. This low-inflammatory ssPalmO-LNP platform thus supports safe, rapid vaccine development against emerging H5N1 viruses with pandemic potential.

title: Cross-clade protection against human H5N1 isolates by a clade 2.3.4.4b HA mRNA vaccine in mice.

abstract: The human ileal epithelium forms a critical interface governing interactions with luminal microorganisms and nanomaterials, yet physiologically relevant in vitro models with accessible apical surfaces remain limited. Here, human apical-out ileoids derived from healthy ileal biopsies are established as a platform that recapitulates the architecture and complexity of the native ileal epithelium. Assessment of donor- and passage-dependent variability identifies a representative ileoid line and a robust culture window. Integrated proteomic, imaging, ultrastructural, and functional analyses demonstrate preservation of key epithelial features, including brush-border organization, barrier integrity, absorptive capacity, and multiple endocytic pathways. Intact ileoids internalize nanoparticles of distinct surface charge, including empty lipid nanoparticles compositionally matched to approved mRNA vaccine formulations, establishing that uptake can be quantified across an unperturbed apical surface. This uptake is restrained by a retained mucin-rich glycocalyx. Cleavage of surface-attached mucins selectively enhances uptake of negatively charged nanoparticles, leaving near-neutral and positively charged nanoparticles unchanged, and increasing entry of Salmonella bacteria. These findings reveal the glycocalyx as a charge-selective regulator of epithelial uptake. In conclusion, our study provides a foundation for nanoparticle-epithelium investigations using human apical-out ileoids, and a versatile, translationally relevant platform for nanomedicine delivery, host-microbe interactions, and epithelial transport.

title: Apical-Out Ileal Organoids: A Versatile Platform for Probing Gut-Nanomaterial Interactions

abstract: Lipid-based nanoparticles (LNPs) are leading synthetic delivery systems for the functional delivery of small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) and mRNA vaccines in vivo. However, current state-of-the-art LNPs, although designed with near optimal properties of fusogenicity for target cell entry and release of RNA APIs, possess suboptimal colloidal stability and biocompatibility due to limited uses of polyethylene glycol-lipids (PEG-lipids) in formulation. We overcome this shortcoming here with novel pH-triggered RNA-LNPs (ZK2 LNPs) that comprise PEG-lipid oxime conjugates (5 mol%), prepared in situ using pH-reversible aminoxy-aldehyde click chemistry. Using mass spectrometry and electron microscopy, ZK2 LNPs are shown colloidally stable in PBS at neutral pH but subject (between pH 7 and 6) to pH-triggered PEG-shedding, from hydrolytic cleavage of PEG-lipid oxime conjugates, and pH-sensitive lipid phase changes. These same mild acid-induced physicochemical changes appear to promote increasingly efficient fusion of ZK2 LNPs with endosome model extracellular vesicles (EVs) at pH values in tune with early endosome pH changes (pH 6.8 to 6), hence explaining in confocal microscopy studies how ZK2 LNPs drive endosome lysis then RNA release into the cytoplasm of HepG2 cells in vitro, following cell entry by endocytosis. Finally, ZK2 LNPs mediate effective functional hepatitis B virus (HBV) gene silencing in the HepG2.2.15 model of chronic HBV (CHB) infection and demonstrate excellent LNP tolerability in vivo, too. Therefore, ZK2 LNPs appear to possess unique physicochemical characteristics for colloidal stability, biocompatibility, potential stealth, and efficient RNA API delivery to cytoplasm in target cells, hence could represent a powerful next generation LNP technology.

title: Precise pH-triggered cleavage of PEG-lipid conjugates drives endosomal escape of siRNA from fusogenic lipid-based nanoparticles.

abstract: Targeting microglia with adeno-associated viruses (AAVs) remains challenging because of inefficient transduction, off-target expression, and inconsistent payload performance. Here, we develop an integrated, Cre-independent AAV platform that combines a compact 446-bp microglia-specific regulatory element (MSRE), a high-yield AAV2/9.m capsid, microRNA-mediated neuronal de-targeting, and a microglia-tailored codon-optimization strategy. Following direct intracranial delivery, the optimized vector achieves robust, long-lasting transgene expression with greater than 90% microglial specificity across multiple mouse brain regions, including in an Alzheimer's disease model. With doxorubicin-assisted delivery, the platform also enables efficient and selective microglial targeting in rats, rhesus macaques, and human ex vivo brain slices. Codon optimization supports the expression of otherwise challenging functional payloads, enabling calcium imaging, chemogenetic manipulation, and CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome editing. This cross-species toolkit provides a versatile resource for investigating microglial biology and developing microglia-directed therapeutic strategies.

abstract: Herpes zoster (HZ), caused by varicella-zoster virus (VZV), remains a substantial public health burden, particularly in aging populations, due to the risk of severe complications like postherpetic neuralgia (PHN). While existing vaccines (eg. Shingrix®) have advanced prevention efficiencies, they present notable limitations, such as high reactogenicity and complex manufacturing. mRNA vaccines represent a transformative alternative with rapid manufacturing, precise antigen design, and favorable safety. This review synthesizes the current landscape of mRNA vaccine development for HZ, focusing on the rational design of antigen constructs, innovations in lipid nanoparticle delivery systems, insights from preclinical immunogenicity studies, and the progress of leading candidates into clinical trials. In summary, this review highlights the potential of mRNA vaccines to address the limitations of current options, potentially offering a new paradigm for safer, highly efficacious, and scalable HZ prevention. Continued clinical validation is crucial to realize this potential and alleviate the global disease burden.

abstract: T cells are central mediators of antitumour immunity and are the cellular basis of many successful cancer immunotherapies, including immune checkpoint blockade, T-cell receptor (TCR)-engineered therapies and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells. However, clinical responses remain variable, and many tumours evade or resist T-cell-mediated control. Understanding how T cells recognise tumour cells, deliver cytotoxic signals, produce inflammatory cytokines and shape tumour cell fate is therefore essential for improving modern immunotherapies. In vitro tumour T-cell coculture systems provide a powerful experimental framework for dissecting these processes under controlled conditions. They allow investigators to manipulate antigen specificity, HLA/MHC restriction, tumour genotype, T-cell activation state, cytokine exposure and drug-mediated perturbation in ways that are difficult to achieve in vivo. However, these systems require careful design, because assay outcomes are strongly influenced by tumour model, antigen expression, effector-to-target ratio, assay duration and readout. This guide provides a practical framework for studying tumour T-cell interactions in vitro, with a focus on CD8+ T-cell-mediated tumour recognition and killing. It discusses commonly used mouse and human antigen-specific models, how antigen expression and presentation can be experimentally controlled, T-cell activation and coculture conditions, cytotoxicity assays, immune synapse imaging, competition assays, cytokine-mediated bystander killing, transcriptional profiling, CRISPR perturbation strategies, therapeutic testing and patient-derived models. The aim is to help researchers choose the most appropriate model, experimental setup and readout for the biological question being asked and to avoid common interpretive pitfalls when studying tumour immune sensitivity, resistance and therapeutic response.

abstract: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is a WHO-priority pathogen with high mortality and wide global distribution. A major challenge in CCHFV vaccine development is identifying antigens that induce functional cellular and humoral immunity. We previously showed that the CCHF nucleoprotein (NP) elicits protective responses in mice and non-human primates but does not induce neutralizing antibodies. We therefore systematically screened six chimeric DNA vaccines expressing different CCHF glycoproteins combined with NP. A construct comprising the ectodomain of the glycoprotein Gc and NP elicited robust antibody and T-cell responses to both antigens. The Gc-NP gene was subsequently developed as a lipid nanoparticle-formulated mRNA vaccine using a scalable manufacturing pipeline. Gc-NP mRNA-LNP induced robust antigen-specific humoral and cellular responses comparable to those elicited by the corresponding DNA vaccine, despite the substantially lower dose. Both vaccine approaches generated Gc-directed neutralizing antibody responses against CCHFV pseudovirus and protected mice against homologous Hoti and heterologous IbAr10200 strain challenge. These findings demonstrate that systematic antigen screening combined with genetic vaccine platforms can identify a potent multi-antigen CCHF vaccine candidate.

abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) exhibit superior intrinsic stability and lower immunogenicity compared with linear RNAs, rendering them promising modalities for biomedical and biotechnological applications. Here, we establish the HARBOR (Human-Archaeal RNA Backbone for Overexpression of circular RNA) system, an engineered endogenous circRNA expression platform integrating a human precursor transfer RNA (pre-tRNA) scaffold with an archaeal Bulge-Helix-Bulge (BHB) motif. HARBOR repurposes the endogenous tRNA splicing machinery to generate chimeric pre-tRNA intermediates, which are rapidly degraded following processing, while producing circRNAs ranging from hundreds of nucleotides to 8 knt in cells and in vivo. Notably, it enables robust production of large-sized circRNAs with yields nearly 80-fold than the intronic complementary sequence-mediated back-splicing (3D5) system and can drive protein expression from translatable circRNAs at an efficiency close to 20-fold than the Tornado system. Such prominent properties support diverse applications of HARBOR, including producing therapeutic aptamers targeting PKR-associated neuroinflammation and pathological TDP-43 condensation, as well as protein-coding circRNAs encoding adenine base editors for genome editing and MYOD1 for fibroblast-to-myocyte trans-differentiation. Collectively, HARBOR represents a versatile, scalable, and user-friendly platform that unifies circRNA-based aptamer and protein expression applications, advancing circRNA-enabled engineering and biomedical applications.

abstract: β-Thalassemia, a major genetic disease affecting the global population, has seen new strategies being pursued in terms of curative attempts directed at the specific gene defect present. Iron chelation therapy and lifelong blood transfusions have historically been used to treat β-thalassemia, a severe hereditary hemoglobin condition marked by decreased or missing β-globin chain synthesis. These methods have significantly increased patient survival, but they do not offer a permanent solution and are linked to serious side effects and a high cost of care. With a focus on hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), lentiviral gene-addition treatment, and future genome-editing techniques, this study outlines new and creative methods to long-term disease correction in β-thalassemia. Although allogeneic HSCT is still a proven treatment option, its use is constrained by the availability of donors, graft-related issues, and transplant-related hazards. Autologous hematopoietic stem cell-based gene therapy has become a significant substitute, provided the possibility of long-term transfusion independence while prevented graft-versus-host disease. With the creation of exagamglogene autotemcel (exa-cel; Casgevy), which reactivates fetal hemoglobin expression through modification of the BCL11A erythroid enhancer and has shown significant rates of sustained transfusion independence in eligible patients with transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia, CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing has recently marked a significant clinical milestone. Notwithstanding these encouraging developments, myeloablative conditioning, long-term safety and durability, high treatment costs, complicated manufacturing requirements, and restricted accessibility continue to be major obstacles, especially in low- and middle-income nations. All things considered, the therapeutic landscape for β-thalassemia is changing from lifelong supportive management to potentially curative and transformative interventions; however, the wider application of these cutting-edge therapies depends on ongoing long-term evaluation and efforts to increase affordability and global accessibility.

abstract: Gene delivery and the various routes of administration used to deliver viral vectors constitute a rapidly evolving field, with recent success in restoring hearing in children with OTOF variants in ongoing clinical otoferlin trials. With the rise of gene therapy for major hereditary hearing disorders, both syndromic and nonsyndromic, there has been parallel progress in the development of new delivery methods. Advances in intratympanic injection of antibiotics and corticosteroids, along with nearly half a century of experience in cochlear implantation surgery, have enabled multiple local and systemic approaches to access the inner ear. Recent industry investment in gene therapy and delivery technologies has accelerated scientific progress, underscoring the need for continuous evaluation of the most suitable gene delivery strategies for different causes of hearing loss. Although most gene delivery in animal models has been performed via round window membrane injection, yielding promising results in cochlear hair cell transduction, potential drawbacks remain for clinical translation-particularly limited vector distribution, which may result in a basal-to-apical gradient. Venting procedures such as stapes footplate fenestration or canalostomy have been explored to mitigate these limitations, and recent intrathecal or even in utero injections have been investigated as alternative approaches. Hearing loss can be inherited in multiple ways, and patient treatment with gene delivery, or even the type of gene therapy itself, may vary with the recent success of CRISPR/Cas-based editing tools. Understanding the genetic etiology of inner ear disorders has facilitated the identification of therapeutic targets and innovative delivery approaches. This review summarizes the current understanding of delivery routes for gene therapy, highlighting their respective strengths and limitations as demonstrated in translational and clinical research to date. Furthermore, it examines advances in drug delivery and clinical applications in the context of emerging therapeutics, providing an integrated overview and perspective on the future direction of gene delivery strategies.
