abstract: Haploinsufficiency of progranulin (resulting from mutations in the GRN gene) is a major genetic cause of frontotemporal dementia (FTD), which is characterized by profound changes in personality and behavior, progressive impairments in executive function, speech, language and/or movement, TDP-43 pathology, lysosomal dysfunction, and neuroinflammation. Studies in progranulin-deficient mouse models have demonstrated the critical role of neuroinflammation in disease pathogenesis, as deletion of NF-kB or complement factors prevents FTD-associated behavioral deficits. While progranulin is known to be anti-inflammatory, the precise molecular mechanism by which its deficiency triggers inflammatory cascades remain unclear. Here, we investigate the involvement of the NLRP3 inflammasome in progranulin-deficient models, including mice, human microglial cells, and patient fibroblasts. In Grn mice, we found increased levels of several inflammasome-related proteins, including procaspase-1 and cleaved IL-1{beta}. Similarly, GRN knockout (KO) microglia cells showed significant increases in levels of procaspase-1, NLRP3, and cleaved IL-1{beta}. Moreover, KO cells had increased NLRP3 oligomerization, suggesting that progranulin negatively regulates inflammasome assembly. We also investigated the potential link between lysosomal dysfunction and NLRP3 inflammasome activation in progranulin deficiency. We found that pharmacological inhibition of cathepsin B reduced NLRP3 inflammasome oligomerization as well as inflammatory cytokine expression in GRN KO cells. Additionally, siRNA knockdown of cathepsin B reduced levels of procaspase-1 and cleaved IL-1{beta} in GRN KO cells. Finally, we found that heterozygous GRN fibroblasts exhibited similar increases in procaspase-1 and cleaved IL-1{beta} levels, and these increases were corrected by treatment with an antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) that increase progranulin protein levels. Overall, our results demonstrate that progranulin deficiency promotes NLRP3 inflammasome assembly and activity through cathepsin B-mediated signaling, thereby establishing a mechanistic link between lysosomal dysfunction and increased inflammation. The ability of the GRN-targeting ASO to correct NLRP3-mediated inflammation highlights a promising therapeutic strategy for FTD-GRN and inflammation in other neurodegenerative disorders linked to progranulin deficiency.

abstract:
A novel zoonotic coronavirus was discovered in Wuhan (Hubei Province, China) mid-December 2019 and was named severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). The virus rapidly spread to the rest of the world, including Europe and explicitly affects the respiratory system, generating Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19).

This study is a monocentric interventional prospective and retrospective cohort study. After signing a written informed consent, participants will be recruited for questionnaire completion and blood sampling. Sample storage and analysis will be performed at the laboratory of microbiology of the UZ Brussel.

To document SARS-CoV-2 seroprevalence and seroconversion among employees of the UZ Brussel after mRNA vaccination for SARS-CoV-2, namely at 8 weeks after first vaccination, 6 months after first vaccination and 12 months after first vaccination.
description:
A novel zoonotic coronavirus was discovered in Wuhan (Hubei Province, China) mid-December 2019 and was named severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). The virus rapidly spread to the rest of the world, including Europe and explicitly affects the respiratory system, generating Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19).

UZ Brussel employees presenting symptoms suggestive of COVID-19 are offered to be tested with real-time PCR on nasopharyngeal swabs. As asymptomatic infections have been described and as the PCR can be negative when taken late after onset of symptoms, serologic tests can be performed. The SARS-CoV 2003 epidemic demonstrated that serological assays were a useful diagnostic tool of non-acute infections. Although it is still uncertain whether convalescing patients have a risk of re-infection, recent data suggest that SARS-CoV-2 antibodies could protect at least for some time from subsequent viral exposures.

As the COVID-19 pandemic had devastating medical, economic and social consequences, safe and effective prophylactic vaccines were urgently needed. And thus several candidate vaccines against SARS-CoV-2 have been developed. During the first weeks of the vaccination campaign, the health care workers of the UZ Brussel, were invited to receive the BNT162b2 (Pfizer) vaccine.

Consequently, the investigators aim to prospectively document the SARS-CoV-2 seroprevalence and seroconversion among vaccinated employees of the UZ Brussel, at three different time points, namely 6 weeks (+/- 2 weeks; T1), 6 months (+/- 1 month; T2) and 12 months (+/- 1 month; T3) after the second vaccination.

abstract: Spatiotemporal precision remains a critical challenge against the gene editing technology used for disease treatment. We herein developed a tumor cell-selective CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing system by introducing a complementary single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) containing apurinic/apyrimidinic (AP) sites (AP-ssDNA) along the target region of single-guided RNA (sgRNA). The engineered hybrid (AP-ssDNA/sgRNA) could tracelessly release the native sgRNA in tumor cells due to cleavage of AP-ssDNA by the overexpressed apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease 1 (APE1), thus enabling tumor-selective gene editing. Subsequently, a biodegradable lipid nanoparticle based on dynamic covalent bonding was developed to codeliver Cas9-encoding mRNA (mCas9) with AP-ssDNA/sgRNA targeting the SUV39H1 gene, which mediated silence of cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS) methylation to activate stimulator of interferon genes (STING) and enhanced antitumor immunity. As thus, when coupled with radiotherapy, the gene editing platform provoked robust antitumor efficacy in B16F10 xenograft tumor-bearing mice. This study provides a versatile paradigm for conditionally controlled gene editing and highlights the therapeutic potential of cGAS demethylation in reactivating cGAS-STING pathway for antitumor immunotherapy.

abstract: The ever-increasing global demand for food and feed, coupled with population growth and climate change, necessitates the development of high-yielding and stress-resilient crops. CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) technology has emerged as a transformative genome-editing tool due to its efficiency, precision, and ability to generate targeted genetic modifications. This review highlights recent advances in CRISPR genome editing, including base editing, prime editing, and novel Cas variants, together with emerging approaches such as epigenome editing, mitochondrial genome editing, and hypercompact Cas systems, and their applications in improving crop productivity, stress tolerance, and nutritional quality. In food and feed crops, these applications also include crop-specific priorities such as grain and nutritional quality in food crops and digestibility, forage quality, and mineral bioavailability in feed and forage crops. Particular emphasis is placed on the complex intellectual property (IP) landscape surrounding CRISPR technologies, including patents on editing systems, delivery platforms, and proprietary vectors. These intellectual property barriers can restrict research access, technology transfer, and commercialization, particularly in developing countries. The review further discusses patent limitations, licensing frameworks, and strategies to enhance equitable global access through collaborative approaches such as non-exclusive licensing, humanitarian licensing, indigenous technology development, and international partnerships. Overall, the review underscores the need to balance innovation, intellectual property protection, and global accessibility to ensure that CRISPR-based technologies contribute effectively to worldwide food and feed security and sustainable agriculture.

abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing has emerged as one of the most promising strategies in precision medicine applied to ophthalmology. Although its initial development focused on inherited retinal diseases, recent advances have increasingly targeted anterior segment disorders, including herpetic keratitis, hereditary corneal dystrophies, and genetically associated glaucoma. The ability to modify specific DNA or RNA sequences enables direct intervention in molecular pathways involved in inflammatory, degenerative, and infectious disease progression. This review summarizes the biological basis of CRISPR-Cas systems and discusses the main preclinical and translational findings related to corneal and glaucomatous diseases. Current limitations, including off-target effects, immunogenicity, and challenges associated with molecular delivery into ocular tissues, are also addressed. Available evidence suggests that CRISPR-Cas9 may significantly transform the future management of multiple anterior segment diseases.

abstract:
AIM: To investigate the functional significance of Hippo-YAP signaling in platelet activation and thrombosis.
METHODS: Expression and phosphorylation of YAP were examined in platelets exposed to physiological agonists as well as mechanical cues (adhesion to matrices having varying stiffness and activation of mechanosensitive channel Piezo1). Involvements of LATS kinase and RhoA-ROCK-actomyosin axis in YAP signaling were evaluated. Effect of pharmacological inhibition of YAP on platelet activation parameters (αIIbβ3 activation, adhesion, α-granule secretion, extracellular vesicle release, and fibrin clot retraction) were studied ex vivo. Contribution of YAP to pathological thrombosis was further investigated in a murine model in vivo. YAP activity was also assessed in platelets obtained from patients diagnosed with acute coronary syndrome.
KEY FINDINGS: Platelets expressed mRNA transcript as well as peptide of YAP, whose phosphorylation (at Ser-127) was modulated in response to physiological agonists and mechanical stimuli. Adhesion to immobilized matrix, Piezo1 stimulation, and exposure to agonists markedly enhanced YAP expression. Concomitantly, these factors prompted dephosphorylation of YAP, suggestive of YAP functional impairment, driven by the upstream LATS kinase and RhoA-ROCK-actomyosin signaling axis. Inhibition of YAP impaired key platelet functions ex vivo, that included integrin αIIbβ3 activation, adhesion, α-granule secretion, extracellular vesicle release, and fibrin clot retraction, and exerted marked protection against pathological thrombosis in a murine model in vivo. Consistent with above, platelets obtained from patients diagnosed with acute coronary syndrome were found to harbour enhanced YAP activity.
CONCLUSION: These findings underscore a contributing role of YAP in thrombogenesis, highlighting its potential as an antiplatelet therapeutic target.

abstract: Retinoblastoma is a rare pediatric intraocular malignancy for which intravitreal administration offers a clinically attractive route for localized therapy owing to its minimally invasive nature and direct access to intraocular tumors. However, efficient intravitreal delivery of nucleic acids remains challenging because the protein-poor vitreous microenvironment restricts nanoparticle transport and subsequent intracellular delivery. Conventional lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), which have been primarily developed for systemic administration, are therefore not necessarily suited to this unique biological environment. Here, we developed a C12-200-containing lipid nanoparticle (CLNP) engineered for efficient intravitreal gene delivery through systematic optimization of lipid composition. The optimized CLNP exhibited favorable diffusion within the vitreous, efficient intracellular mRNA delivery, and reduced dependence on extracellular protein-assisted uptake under vitreous-mimetic conditions. To demonstrate the therapeutic versatility of the platform, human RB transcriptional corepressor 1 mRNA and triptolide were co-delivered as representative gene and small-molecule therapeutics. CLNP-mediated co-delivery of hRB1 mRNA and triptolide produced greater antiproliferative activity than either monotherapy in vitro and markedly suppressed tumor progression in an orthotopic retinoblastoma model following a single intravitreal administration, with no detectable abnormalities in retinal function, structure, or apoptosis during the evaluation period. Collectively, this study establishes a vitreous-oriented lipid engineering strategy that simultaneously improves extracellular transport through the vitreous and intracellular nucleic acid delivery, providing a broadly applicable platform for localized gene delivery and combination gene-drug therapy for ocular diseases.

abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have emerged as the most widely used non-viral gene delivery system, particularly for mRNA therapeutics. However, predominant hepatic accumulation and poor local delivery remain major barriers to their broader application. To address this challenge, we employed a design of experiments (DOE) strategy to systematically refine LNP composition and identified an optimized formulation, SM102M. Compared with the parental SM102 formulation, SM102M markedly reduced liver-associated signal after both intramuscular and intravenous administration, while preserving or enhancing local expression after local delivery. Across multiple local administration routes, including intramuscular, intracerebroventricular, and intravitreal injection, SM102M supported localized gene delivery and gene editing with minimal liver-associated signal. Mechanistically, the altered biodistribution of SM102M was associated with reduced apolipoprotein E (ApoE) binding, lower systemic exposure, and diminished lysosomal escape in hepatocytes. SM102M also showed favorable tolerability and maintained local delivery performance under repeated administration. Together, these findings establish DOE as a practical framework for rational LNP engineering and identify a formulation with reduced hepatic reporter expression and improved local delivery performance.

abstract: Over the past decade, CRISPR-Cas based biosensors have emerged as sensitive, specific and programmable platforms for nucleic acid detection, with applications ranging from diagnostic tools, environmental monitoring and various applications in fundamental research. The vast majority of these biosensors are currently limited to in vitro applications, highlighting the need for cellular platforms. Here, we provide a perspective on the potential of type III CRISPR-Cas systems as a platform for real-time RNA biosensing in living cells. We discuss the unique properties that distinguish type III from other CRISPR-Cas types, including their intrinsic cyclic oligoadenylate (cOA) signal amplification cascade, PAM-free RNA targeting and the extensive biochemical diversity of their downstream CARF and SAVED effector proteins. We outline the fundamental design principles of a genetically encoded type III cellular biosensor, comprising a programmable guide RNA, a multi-subunit sensing complex and a cOA-sensing effector protein capable of generating optical or electrochemical readout signals. A remaining challenge for type III cellular biosensors is the inherent cytotoxicity of canonical cOA-activated effectors. We propose several strategies to re-engineer these outputs towards non-cytotoxic reporter systems. While cellular biosensors present a natural route toward in vivo sensing, they face many challenges beyond the choice of the output signal and hardware strategy. We conclude that type III CRISPR-Cas is a promising platform for programmable real-time RNA sensing in living cells, utilizing its diverse modular effector outputs, representing a significant expansion of the CRISPR biosensor toolkit, while emphasizing appropriate deployment scenarios that enables full potential of these biosensors.

abstract: MASLD (Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease), is a chronic liver condition marked by excessive fat buildup (steatosis) in liver cells, linked to at least one metabolic risk factor like obesity, type 2 diabetes, high blood lipids, or hypertension. Vitamin E serves as a recommended antioxidant therapy for select MASLD patients. It reduces liver inflammation markers such as ALT and AST, alongside benefits in steatosis and MASH resolution. Silymarin has clinical evidence supports its use as an adjunctive hepatoprotective agent due to antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antifibrotic effects.
description: To evaluate the efficacy of vitamin E (800 IU/day) versus silymarin (420 mg/day, divided TID) in modulating MASLD-associated mRNA expression, NLRP3 inflammasome levels, and MDA in adult patients with MASLD

abstract: Genome engineering via CRISPR/Cas9 has been widely applied in biological research and developing gene therapies. However, genome editing flexibility is strongly constrained by the position and quality of guide RNAs relative to the intended edit: desired edit sites are frequently positioned far from efficient protospacer adjacent motifs (PAM). SMART (Silently Mutate And Repair Template) technique relaxes this constraint by silently mutating the gap between the Cas9 cut and the edit in the repair donor, preserving the encoded protein while expanding the usable guide-RNA design space. Designing such donors manually requires coordinated reasoning over transcript structure, reading frame, candidate protospacers, codon usage, homology arms and the expected edited allele. Auto-SMART is a web platform that automates this process for CRISPR/Cas9-mediated insertion, deletion, point mutation and sequence replacement in coding exons and in introns. Users choose a genome assembly, search a gene symbol or transcript, select a modification site and select an editing operation. Auto-SMART finds nearby Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9 (SpCas9) guides, ranks them by predicted on-target activity and cut-to-edit geometry, builds repair templates with synonymous substitutions, automatically recodes residual on-target sites to prevent re-cutting and renders interpretable panels for the target locus, donor template and locus after HDR, together with a downloadable report and a Primer3 genotyping handoff. The web application for Auto-SMART is freely available at https://auto-smart.chuanping.org/ .

abstract: The purpose of this trial is to assess the safety and relative efficacy of CVXGA (CVXGA50), a KP.2 containing vaccine, compared to COMIRNATY® (COVID-19 Vaccine, mRNA; 2024-2025 Formula), a currently approved COVID-19 vaccine in the prevention of symptomatic, RT-PCR-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection. The trial will enroll up to 434 healthy participants.

description:
This is a double-blind, active comparator-controlled Phase 2b study to evaluate the efficacy, immunogenicity, and safety study in which eligible adult participants will be randomized 1:1 to receive CVXGA (CVXGA50) or COMIRNATY.

Number of Participants:

The proposed enrollment for this study is approximately 434 participants, that includes 16 participants enrolled in Sentinel Cohort 1 and Sentinel Cohort 2 (8 participants in each cohort).

Treatment Assignment:

Participants in Sentinel Cohort 1 and Sentinel Cohort 2 will be assigned to receive a single dose of CVXGA (CVXGA50) intranasally and will not receive an IM placebo.

All other participants in the study will be randomized 1:1 to receive a single dose of CVXGA (CVXGA50) intranasally (plus a single dose of IM placebo), or a single dose of IM COMIRNATY (plus a single dose of intranasal placebo).

Study visits: Participants will be asked to complete approximately 6-7 clinic visits, over a period of approximately 12 months duration per participant.

* Clinical signs at rest indicative of severe systemic illness (respiratory rate ≥30 breaths per minute, heart rate ≥125 beats per minute, SpO2 ≤93% on room air or PaO2/FiO2 \<300 mm Hg)
* Respiratory failure (defined as needing high-flow oxygen, noninvasive ventilation, mechanical ventilation, or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation \[ECMO\])
* Evidence of shock (systolic blood pressure \[SBP\] \<90 mm Hg, diastolic blood pressure \[DBP\] \<60 mm Hg, or requiring vasopressors)
* Significant acute renal, hepatic, or neurologic dysfunction
* Admission to an intensive care unit (ICU)
* Death

abstract:
Background:

X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (XSCID) is a rare inherited disorder that affects the immune system. It is caused by a change in the IL2RG gene. Researchers are investigating a new type of gene therapy for people with XSCID. This technique, called base-edited stem cell transplants, involves collecting a person s own stem cells, editing the genes to repair IL2RG gene, and returning the edited cells to the person.

Objective:

To test base-edited stem cell transplants in people with XSCID.

Eligibility:

People aged 3 years and older with XSCID.

Design:

Participants will be screened. They will have a physical exam. They may give blood, urine, and stool samples. They may have tests of their heart and lung function. They may have fluid and cells drawn from their bone marrow.

Participants will undergo apheresis. Blood will be taken from the body through a needle inserted into 1 arm. The blood will pass through a machine that separates out the stem cells. The remaining blood will be returned to the body through a different needle. The collected stem cells will undergo gene editing.

Participants will be admitted to the hospital 1 week before treatment. They will receive a central line: A flexible tube will be inserted into a large vein. This tube will be used to administer drugs and draw blood during their stay. They will receive drugs to prepare their bodies for the treatment.

The base-edited stem cells will be infused through the central line. Participants will remain in the hospital for at least 3 weeks while they recover.

Follow-up visits will continue for 15 years.

description:
Study Description:

This is a phase 1/2, non-randomized study of a single infusion of autologous hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells base-edited to repair interleukin 2 receptor gamma (IL2RG) mutations (BE-HSPC IL2RG) in 18 participants with X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (X-SCID).

Primary Objective:

Evaluate the safety of treatment with BE-HSPC IL2RG in participants with X-SCID.

Secondary Objectives:

Evaluate efficacy of treatment with BE-HSPC IL2RG in participants with X-SCID.

Exploratory Objectives:

1. Evaluate off-target (OT) editing activity.
2. Compare outcomes of immune reconstitution with lentivector (LV) gene therapy.

Primary Endpoint:

Safety of treatment with BE-HSPC IL2RG, by quantifying frequency and severity of adverse events (AEs) related to study agent from infusion to 12 months after infusion.

Secondary Endpoints (24 months post-study agent infusion):

1. Percentage of participants with \>=5% mutation-repaired myeloid cells.
2. Editing efficiency in peripheral blood cells (such as T, B, and natural killer \[NK\] cells).
3. Immune reconstitution:

   1. T, B, and NK cell number improvement from baseline.
   2. Emergence of naive T cells and CD31+ recent thymic emigrants.
   3. B-cell function: immunoglobulin (Ig) production.
   4. Specific responses to vaccines.
4. Clinical efficacy: improvement from baseline problems such as recurrent infection, chronic norovirus, protein-losing enteropathy, gastrointestinal complaints, growth failure, malnutrition, or immune dysregulation.
5. Frequency and severity of all study agent-related AEs and serious adverse events (SAEs) from time of study product infusion.

Exploratory Endpoints:

1. Evaluate for frequency of off-targets (OTs) by high-throughput sequencing (HTS) of the target mutation at 2 years post-infusion.
2. Compare rates of immune reconstitution with LV-X-SCID gene therapy.

abstract:
This is a randomised, actively controlled Phase IIb trial to evaluate the safety and pharmacodynamics (PD) of two blinded doses of subcutaneously administered vortosiran and open-label apixaban in patients with AF.

The trial consists of three groups including 50 participants each. The participants will be randomized to either the low dose group or the high dose group receiving vortosiran or to the group receiving apixaban. The treatment will be open-label for vortosiran vs apixaban. The vortosiran dose will be blinded to patients and investigators.

Both the low- and the high-dose group will receive two doses of vortosiran, the first dose at Day X and the second at Day Y. After 24 weeks, at the end of the vortosiran treatment period, the participants will start an open-label part of the trial and will be switched to standard-of-care apixaban treatment until Week 64 (End of Trial; EOT). Participants in the open-label apixaban arm will receive apixaban as standard of care during the entire trial.

description:
Atrial fibrillation (AF) is among the most prevalent cardiovascular conditions, affecting approximately 2 4% of the adult population worldwide. AF represents the most common sustained supraventricular arrhythmia and is associated with substantial morbidity, mortality, and health-care burden. Patients with AF are at an elevated risk of thromboembolic complications, particularly ischemic stroke and systemic embolism, while also facing an increased risk of bleeding associated with long-term antithrombotic therapy administered to prevent these complications. The principal aim of management in AF is to prevent stroke while minimizing haemorrhagic risk through careful risk stratification for both thromboembolic risk and bleeding risk, and informed and individualised treatment selections.

According to current guideline recommendations, oral anticoagulation is recommended for stroke prevention and may be guided by CHA2DS2 -VASc clinical risk assessment tool. Nonvitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulants (NOACs, also referred to as direct oral anticoagulants, or DOACs) are preferred over vitamin K antagonists (VKAs) in most cases due to their superior safety profile and lower incidence of intracranial bleeding. Bleeding risk can be assessed using validated tools such as HAS-BLED, and modifiable risk factors should be addressed to reduce overall treatment-related complications.

Despite a superior efficacy-safety profile of NOACs relative to VKAs, patients treated with NOACs remain at residual risk for stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular mortality. Furthermore, although NOACs are associated with reduced rates of intracranial haemorrhage compared with VKAs, they still confer a considerable risk of major bleeding and clinically relevant non-major bleeding events. Consequently, the clinical need for strategies that further optimize the balance between thromboembolic prevention and bleeding risk in patients with AF remains.

Recent advances have positioned coagulation factor XI (FXI) inhibition as a promising strategy in anti-thrombotic drug development. FXI is a crucial element of the intrinsic coagulation pathway, and genetic FXI deficiency (haemophilia C) is typically associated with only mild bleeding even in complete deficiency, suggesting the potential for improved safety compared to conventional anti-thrombotic drugs by disengaging physiologic haemostasis from pathologic, intraluminal thrombosis. FXI inhibition reliably prolongs activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) in vitro, and epidemiological studies demonstrate that inherited FXI deficiency confers protection against venous thromboembolism (VTE) and ischemic stroke. Conversely, elevated circulating activated FXI (FXIa) is linked to higher risks of ischemic stroke, VTE, and acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Contemporary research utilizing coagulometric assays has confirmed FXIa and tissue factor activation in patients with stable coronary artery disease, ACS of less than 12 hours' duration, and heart failure, reinforcing FXI's role as a pathogenic factor in these conditions.

From the patient perspective, the limitations of current DOAC-based strategies extend beyond rare catastrophic haemorrhage to include a spectrum of patient-relevant bleeding and treatment burdens that erode quality of life and adherence. Easy bruising, epistaxis, gingival bleeding, menorrhagia, and minor gastrointestinal bleeding are often labelled nuisance or non-major events in clinical trials, but patients describe these as anxiety-provoking, stigmatizing, and disruptive to daily activities. Such events, together with polypharmacy, twice-daily dosing for some agents, drug drug interactions, and the need for uninterrupted long-term therapy, frequently lead to missed doses, dose reductions, or unsupervised discontinuation of DOACs, which in turn compromises stroke protection at the population level. In parallel, important patient subgroups including those with advanced chronic kidney disease or dialysis, advanced liver disease, prior intracranial haemorrhage, or frailty have been underrepresented in pivotal DOAC trials and often withheld treatment or remain untreated because of bleeding concerns. By targeting FXI, vortosiran has the potential to dissociate pathological thrombosis from physiological haemostasis, and to deliver sustained antithrombotic protection with a lower risk bleeding than currently available therapies and an adherence profile that is better aligned with patients' priorities and lived experience.

Clinical trials targeting FXI inhibition in the context of cardiovascular disease, including AF, are ongoing or recently completed. Several Phase 2 and 3 trials are investigating FXI/FXIa inhibitors by use of different modalities such as monoclonal antibodies and small molecules across multiple high-risk groups, evaluating efficacy and bleeding outcomes against standard anticoagulants for stroke prevention in AF (SPAF). These studies collectively support the notion that FXI/FXIa may be a favourable anticoagulation target, capable of reducing thrombotic events with a lower side effect profile, especially bleeding, compared to traditional agents. However, while several trials confirm safety advantages, data on efficacy remain to be further demonstrated, necessitating continued research focus. Vortosiran is an N-acetyl galactosamine (GalNAc) conjugated small interfering ribonucleic acid (siRNA), enabling highly specific and highly durable enrichment of the siRNA in hepatocytes, offering a modality specifically inhibiting the production of FXI. Vortosiran is under development to achieve a durable antithrombotic effect by reducing the levels of FXI.

The rationale for the current trial is based on data from multiple Phase 2 and 3 studies of FXI/FXIa inhibitors that have assessed FXI clotting activity and the effect on venous thrombosis inhibition, and is currently being tested for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation patients. Based on the collective observations for these studies, that FXI clotting activity inhibition translates into a lower risk of thrombosis with a lower risk of bleeding compared to standard of care, the ongoing Phase 3 studies, and that vortosiran treatment can achieve identical or even higher degrees of FXI clotting activity inhibition, there is a rationale that vortosiran could potentially improve benefit-risk balance for stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation compared to standard of care with FXa inhibitors.

abstract:
SUPRA-COPD is a multicenter triple-blind, parallel arm, placebo-controlled randomized controlled trial investigating the efficacy and safety of Urolithin A supplementation during pulmonary rehabilitation in patients with COPD.

The goal of the SUPRA-COPD study is to investigate whether Urolithin A supplementation during pulmonary rehabilitation in patients with COPD improves exercise tolerance, along with several other clinically important outcomes, above and beyond pulmonary rehabilitation participation alone.

Study participation will be approximately 14 weeks and involves in-person visits evaluating exercise tolerance before and after PR.

description:
Pulmonary rehabilitation is a central standard of care intervention for chronic disease management in patients with COPD.

Urolithin A is a natural health product found in berries, pomegranates, and nuts. Urolithin A is approved by the FDA and Health Canada, but no study to date has investigated whether taking Urolithin A improves outcomes in patients with COPD. In previous studies in people without COPD, Urolithin A has been found to stimulate the cellular process known as mitophagy, improving the function of mitochondria, as well as functional capacity. In patients with COPD, it is therefore possible that Urolithin A may lead to improved exercise capacity and muscle strength.

Urolithin A, in combination with pulmonary rehabilitation, may lead to a greater benefit in patients with COPD in terms of exercise capacity and other important health outcomes than pulmonary rehabilitation alone.

Patients with COPD participating in a standard pulmonary rehabilitation program are being recruited for this study. Study participants will be randomly assigned and provided either with Urolithin A or with a visually identical placebo, to be taken every day during the 8-week pulmonary rehabilitation program. Study outcomes will then be compared between the Urolithin A group and the placebo group.

abstract: Hearing loss affects millions worldwide, yet hearing aids and cochlear implants have major limitations. mRNA-based gene therapy could address the underlying molecular causes, but lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery in the inner ear remains underexplored and its biodistribution has not been systematically characterized. Here we establish and scale up an mRNA-encapsulated LNP formulation using a design-of-experiments (DoE) approach built on predefined critical quality attributes, and map the route-dependent distribution of reporter mRNA expression in the neonatal mouse cochlea. In HEI-OC1 auditory cells, mRNA-loaded LNPs produced a higher proportion of reporter-expressing cells and a more uniform distribution of expression than the cationic reagent Lipofectamine at a matched mRNA dose, while total reporter protein was comparable and metabolic viability was not reduced. We then compared cochlear distribution following round window membrane (RWM) delivery versus scala media administration. RWM delivery produced widespread reporter expression in perilymph-exposed compartments-the spiral ligament, the scala vestibuli and scala tympani regions, the stria vascularis and the spiral ganglion region-with no detectable expression in hair cells. Scala media injection produced a more restricted pattern, largely confined to the cuticular plate of inner and outer hair cells and part of the outer sulcus, with no expression in the spiral ganglion region or auditory nerve, indicating that this route does not distribute beyond the endolymphatic compartment. These results define the cochlear compartments accessible to LNP-mediated mRNA delivery and the dependence of that access on administration route, and provide the delivery map required for the design of LNP-based mRNA strategies in the inner ear.

abstract: Senescence has been shown to contribute to the progression of aging-related diseases including degenerative disc disease (DDD). However, the mechanisms regulating senescence in the intervertebral disc (IVD) and other tissues/diseases remain poorly understood. Recently, ZNF865 (BLST) was identified as a previously uncharacterized zinc finger protein that regulates a wide array of genes related to protein processing, cell senescence, and DNA damage repair. Here, we show that ZNF865 expression decreases with age and pathology in human and mouse IVD samples. Utilizing CRISPR-guided gene modulation, we show that ZNF865 is necessary for healthy cell function and is a critical protein in regulating senescence and DNA damage in IVD cells, with implications for a wide range of tissues and organs. We also demonstrate that downregulation of ZNF865 induces senescence in asymptomatic human nucleus pulposus (NP) cells. Conversely, restoration in degenerative NP cells mitigates senescence, SASP expression, and DNA damage, enhances ECM anabolism, and restores chromatin accessibility and gene expression to a healthy state. In vivo, CRISPRi of ZNF865 induces disc degeneration and painful behaviors. Collectively, our findings establish ZNF865 as a novel regulator of genome stability and a potential therapeutic target for mediating senescence/DNA damage in aging related diseases.

abstract: CD8+ T cells directly target and kill cancer cells and are required for effective antitumor immunity. However, CD8+ T cells may become dysfunctional when exposed to chronic antigen stimulation during cancer. Dysfunction is characterized by reduced proliferation, increased expression of inhibitory receptors, and impaired effector function, yet the genetic mechanisms controlling dysfunction remain poorly understood. Therefore, we developed a murine ex vivo chronic stimulation model that recapitulates features of CD8+ T cell dysfunction observed within the tumor microenvironment. By coupling this system with genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 loss-of-function screening, we discovered that the progression of murine CD8+ T cells to a dysfunctional state required eIF4G2, a noncanonical mRNA translation factor. Deletion of eIF4G2 restored CD8+ T cell survival and proliferation during chronic stimulation conditions in vitro. Transcriptomic, proteomic, and flow cytometric analyses revealed that eIF4G2 deletion shifts CD8+ T cell phenotype from a dysfunctional state to a proliferative state. eIF4G2 depletion reduced oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, and accumulation of misfolded protein aggresomes during chronic in vitro stimulation. Finally, eIF4G2-depleted cells mediated enhanced tumor control in a murine model of melanoma. These data suggest that targeting eIF4G2 may promote CD8+ T cell resilience and improve therapeutic antitumor immunity.

title: CRISPR-Cas9 screen identifies eIF4G2 as a regulator of CD8+ T cell dysfunction.

abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and deadly primary brain tumor in adults, characterized by diffuse infiltrative lesions, distinct oncogenic alterations, and a suppressive tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). These traits, however, are not fully recapitulated in current syngeneic murine glioma models, thereby limiting the pre-clinical development of novel therapies. Here we developed murine GBM models with patient-specific mutations that shared striking resemblance with human disease. Mosaic analysis with dual-recombinase mediated cassette exchange (MADR) and CRISPR-Cas9 were leveraged to generate autochthonous tumor models with single-copy somatic transgenesis of murine epidermal growth factor receptor variant III (mEGFRvIII) and loss-of-function mutations commonly observed in GBM. Characterization of a model lacking Pten and Cdkn2a (mEGFRvIII-PC) via histopathologic analyses, functional assays, and single-cell RNA sequencing showed these tumors developed as diffuse, infiltrative lesions with ill-defined margins and a necrotic core. The TIME was primarily comprised of microglia with minimal lymphocyte infiltration, recapitulating patient tumors. Furthermore, these tumors displayed intrinsic resistance to immune checkpoint blockade, potentially due to poor myeloid cell antigen presentation and T cell priming. Additionally, mEGFRvIII-PC cells were the most resistant to antigen-specific T cell-induced cytotoxicity and simultaneously promoted T cell exhaustion, while murine interferon-γ (mIFN-γ) stimulation induced a greater response in vitro with enhanced upregulation of PD-L1 relative to MHC-I. In sum, these findings demonstrate the improved fidelity of the mEGFRvIII-PC model to patient tumors and support its use in developing and refining novel therapeutic paradigms for GBM.

abstract:
The purpose of the study is to quantify and compare the serum nutrient and hormonal profile, and muscle protein synthesis rates, in response to consuming isonitrogenous amounts of a traditional East African meal, mung bean stew with a traditional African corn bread made from two different kinds of maize (whole corn flour or refined).

Specific aim 1: Describe the post-prandial nutrient and hormonal profile in serum in the 3 hours following consumption of a portion of mung bean stew with traditional African corn bread made with either whole grain maize flour or refined maize flour.

Specific aim 2: Compare the ability a portion of mung bean stew and traditional African corn bread made with either whole grain maize flour or refined maize flour to activate mTORC1-specific and whole muscle protein synthesis in an in vitro model of muscle.
description:
Indicators of longevity in humans include skeletal muscle mass and strength. Muscle mass is determined by the balance between myofibrillar protein synthesis and degradation, influenced by diet and physical activity. Muscle strength is closely tied to muscle mass, and activities like weight lifting until failure have been shown to increase muscle protein synthesis, enhancing muscle mass and strength over time. Protein intake is essential for maintaining a positive protein balance and promoting muscle growth. While animal proteins are generally more effective than plant proteins at promoting muscle protein synthesis, many cultures rely on staple plant-based foods, such as maize, rather than animal-based protein sources.

Maize (Zea mays) flour is a leading staple in African diets, where it is consumed in various forms, including porridges and breads like Ugali in East Africa or Fufu in West Africa. The nutritional profile of this corn bread varies greatly depending on whether it is made with refined or whole-grain maize flour. Whole-grain maize flour retains the bran, germ, and endosperm, providing higher fiber, vitamins, and minerals, while refined maize flour primarily contains the endosperm. Although refined maize is lower in fiber, it has a higher proportion of the leucine-rich zein, a major corn protein. These nutritional differences could significantly impact metabolism and overall health.

Given that approximately a fifth of the global population relies on corn meal as a dietary staple, understanding the impact of refined versus whole-grain maize flour on muscle protein synthesis and serum amino acid content could provide valuable insights for dietary guidelines and public health. This study aims to explore these effects, comparing the post-meal nutrient profile and muscle protein synthesis response to traditional African corn bread made with whole-grain versus refined maize flour.

The purpose of the study is to quantify and compare the serum nutrient and hormonal profile and muscle protein synthesis rates in response to consuming isonitrogenous servings of traditional African corn bread made from whole-grain or refined maize flour, paired with mung bean stew.

Specific aim 1: Describe the post-prandial nutrient and hormonal profile in serum in the 3 hours following consumption of a portion of mung bean stew with traditional African corn bread made with either whole grain maize flour or refined maize flour.

Specific aim 2: Compare the ability a portion of mung bean stew and traditional African corn bread made with either whole grain maize flour or refined maize flour to activate mTORC1-specific and whole muscle protein synthesis in an in vitro model of muscle.

Study participants will attend the CTSC Clinical Research Center on two separate occasions.

The two study visits will be scheduled over a 2-week period (i.e., once per week for 2 weeks) at the same time in the morning after an overnight fast of more than 12 hours. Participants will be asked to refrain from vigorous exercise, caffeine, nicotine, and alcohol for 24 hours before each visit. Female participants will schedule their visits within the first two weeks of their menstrual cycle to control for hormone fluctuations that may affect digestion and metabolism.

Upon arrival at the research center for the first test visit, each participant's height and weight will be measured. They will also complete a questionnaire covering their physical activity and dietary habits.

I. Baseline blood draw.

Participants will be seated in individual testing rooms equipped with reclining phlebotomy armchairs. A nurse will insert a 22G catheter into a forearm vein to collect an initial 5 mL baseline blood sample.

II. Test meal.

After baseline blood collection, participants will consume one of the two corn bread test meals. The meal consists of a serving of mung bean stew and an isonitrogenous amount of either whole-grain or refined maize flour-based corn bread:

The food will be weighed before cooking, and an eighth of a teaspoon of salt will be added to enhance palatability and participants will be asked to consume the meal within a 10-minute period, chewing thoroughly. Participants will also drink a 250 mL glass of water with the meal.

III. Postprandial blood draws.

After the test meal, participants will remain at the research site in their testing rooms for 3 hours, where they may bring books or electronic devices to occupy themselves. Five additional 5 mL blood samples will be collected at 30, 60, 90, 120, and 180 minutes post-meal, totaling 30 mL per visit, and 60 mL for participants completing the study.

Blood samples will be collected in 5 mL serum-separating tubes. Samples will clot before centrifugation at 1000 x g for 10 minutes. The serum will then be frozen and stored at -80°C. One milliliter from each serum sample will be used to determine nutrient and hormone concentrations. The remainder will be used for muscle protein synthesis and mTORC1 bioassay analysis.

C2C12Luc cells will be plated in 24-well plates and differentiated over 4 days. Differentiated C2C12 cells will be fasted by washing with PBS and then treating them with Test Media (20% DMEM) for 15 minutes. abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate diethylene glycol monoethyl ether (DEGEE) as an alternative organic solvent to ethanol for mRNA lipid nanoparticle (LNP) manufacture.
METHODS: LNPs composed of distearoyl phosphatidylcholine, cholesterol, a PEGylated lipid and one of four ionizable lipids (SM-102, ALC-0315, Dlin-MC3-DMA or C12-200) were prepared using ethanol or DEGEE. Physicochemical properties were characterized using dynamic light scattering, nanoparticle tracking analysis, single-particle Raman analysis, and asymmetric flow field-flow fractionation. Gas chromatography confirmed solvent removal following purification. Membrane-disruptive activity was evaluated under physiological and endosomal-like pH conditions, and in vivo protein expression was used to assess functional mRNA delivery.
KEY FINDINGS: Across the four LNP formulations tested, DEGEE supported the production of LNPs with physicochemical and biological performance equivalent to ethanol-manufactured LNPs. Both solvents were effectively removed using standard purification workflows, and particle size, polydispersity, zeta potential, encapsulation efficiency, and pH-responsive membrane-disruptive activity were not affected by solvent substitution. In vivo studies further demonstrated comparable protein expression profiles for DEGEE- and ethanol-manufactured LNPs.
CONCLUSIONS: DEGEE is a viable alternative to ethanol for mRNA-LNP manufacture, expanding the solvent options available for formulation development and scalable LNP production.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Metabolic dysregulation is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD), with numerous studies characterizing metabolic pathways associated with AD onset and progression. A limitation of these studies has been a focus on non-Hispanic white participants. Despite evidence that AD prevalence, progression, and biomarkers differ across ethnoracial groups, it remains unclear whether previously identified metabolic dysregulation in AD brains generalizes across populations.
METHODS: We analyzed metabolomics data from 547 postmortem brain tissue samples of Hispanic American, Non-Hispanic African American, and White subjects, providing the largest multiethnic AD brain cohort to date. A metabolome-wide association study examined how relationships between metabolite abundance and AD neuropathology varied by ethnoracial group.
RESULTS: Forty-eight metabolites exhibited significant heterogeneity with tau pathology (Braak stage), with enrichment in tricarboxylic-acid-cycle intermediates and sphingolipid-ceramide pathway lipids, and with metabolite-tau associations driven predominantly by the Hispanic American and non-Hispanic White groups.
DISCUSSION: These findings reveal ethnoracial-specific metabolic signatures of tau pathology and emphasize the need to evaluate emerging therapeutic targets across diverse groups.

abstract: Cisplatin resistance remains a major limitation in the treatment of cervical cancer, with enhanced DNA damage repair contributing to reduced therapeutic sensitivity. The role of STAT5A in coordinating DNA double-strand break repair under therapeutic stress remains unclear. Here, we investigated the role of STAT5A in cisplatin responsiveness using clinical tissue analysis, CRISPR/Cas9-based genetic models, DNA repair assays, and xenograft models. STAT5A depletion sensitized cervical cancer cells to cisplatin, whereas STAT5A overexpression reduced cisplatin sensitivity. Mechanistically, STAT5A showed increased spatial association with γH2AX-positive nuclear regions following cisplatin exposure and transcriptionally promoted RNF8 expression. STAT5A enhanced HR-associated repair through an RNF8-mediated mechanism, as supported by reciprocal genetic experiments and residual DNA damage analysis. STAT5A loss was accompanied by reduced ATM/CHK2 activation, decreased expression of MRN complex components, RNF8 and RAD51, and increased persistence of cisplatin-associated DNA damage. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of STAT5 reduced RNF8 expression, increased DNA damage, and enhanced the antitumor activity of cisplatin in cellular and xenograft models. Together, these findings identify STAT5A-RNF8 signaling as a regulator of HR-associated DNA repair and cisplatin responsiveness in cervical cancer and support further evaluation of this pathway as a therapeutic target.

title: STAT5A-RNF8 signaling regulates homologous recombination repair and cisplatin responsiveness in cervical cancer.

abstract: A substantial proportion of inherited cardiomyopathy cases are driven by mechanisms of haploinsufficiency, where a loss-of-function variant in one allele leads to insufficient protein expression, resulting in loss of normal cardiac function. Current therapies treat symptoms or mitigate risk of complications and do not prevent disease onset or progression. Recently, substantial advances have been made in gene therapies for cardiomyopathies in both preclinical and clinical settings, particularly using viral delivery of whole genes and gene-editing approaches. Alongside these is an emerging area of therapies that aim to upregulate endogenous gene expression. This encompasses a broad array of strategies that may act by removing gene repression or directly enhancing expression, can enhance transcription or translation and may use a variety of modalities such as gene editing or oligonucleotides. Here, we review the mechanisms and current uses of gene upregulation strategies and critically evaluate their advantages and limitations as therapies for inherited cardiomyopathies.

title: Therapeutic upregulation of gene expression in inherited cardiomyopathies from current approaches to future directions.

abstract: Podocyte injury is a convergent driver of glomerular disease progression, yet the genetic determinants that govern podocyte vulnerability to oxidative stress remain incompletely defined. Here, we performed genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screens in differentiated human podocytes exposed to two complementary injury models: Adriamycin (ADR), a clinically relevant inducer of podocyte damage, and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), a direct oxidative stress challenge. Human podocytes were transduced with a genome-wide sgRNA library, differentiated under non-permissive conditions and subjected to optimized stress conditions that imposed selective pressure while preserving library complexity. Across five independent replicates per condition, sequencing-based sgRNA profiling demonstrated high reproducibility, balanced library representation and clear treatment-specific selection. The ADR screen identified 819 depleted and 456 enriched genes, whereas the H2O2 screen identified 277 depleted and 215 enriched genes. Integrated analysis revealed both model-specific dependencies and 27 shared depleted genes across the two injury conditions, implicating stress adaptation, chromatin regulation, mitochondrial metabolism, inflammatory signaling and cytoskeletal organization as candidate processes required for podocyte survival. These genome-wide screens provide a functional framework for prioritizing genes that regulate podocyte resilience to oxidative injury and offer a resource for mechanistic studies of glomerular disease.

title: Genome-wide CRISPR screens identify shared and context-specific regulators of podocyte resistance to oxidative injury.

abstract: Hearing loss is a prevalent sensory disorder with profound social and health impacts. Although hearing aids and cochlear implants can significantly restore auditory perception, they do not address the underlying genetic causes. Inherited forms of hearing loss, often monogenic, are ideal candidates for gene therapy, particularly since over 150 genes have been linked to deafness. Advances in vector engineering and genome editing technologies now enable precise targeting of auditory cells within the inner ear. Technologies such as Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats-Cas systems, base editing, and prime editing offer powerful tools to correct pathogenic variants at their native genomic loci. This review summarizes the current landscape of gene editing approaches for both hereditary and acquired hearing loss, emphasizing key preclinical studies in mouse models encompassing dominant and recessive forms of deafness. We discuss the advantages and limitations of different editing techniques, vector delivery systems, and administration routes, and explore obstacles including editing efficiency, cell-specific targeting, and the translation of these therapies to humans. Collectively, these advances represent a pivotal step toward variant-specific, durable, and potentially curative treatments for hearing loss.

title: Emerging Therapies for Genetic Deafness: The Rise of Precision Gene Editing.

abstract: Melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5 (MDA5), a member of the RIG-I-like receptor family, is a cytoplasmic sensor essential for innate antiviral immunity. MDA5 distinguishes viral RNA from host RNA in part through its ATP hydrolysis activity, which promotes filament turnover on shorter endogenous double-stranded RNAs (dsRNAs). Here, we show that the gain-of-function T331I disease-linked mutation within the ATP-binding pocket disrupts this balance, resulting in constitutive interferon signaling. Through a combination of cryo-electron microscopy (cryoEM), biochemical assays, and cellular analyses, we reveal the extensive network of interactions that precisely position ATP for catalysis in the wild-type MDA5 ATP-binding pocket and also demonstrate that the T331I mutation impairs ATPase activity, thereby stabilizing MDA5-dsRNA complexes and leading to aberrant immune activation. These findings elucidate how MDA5 ATPase activity regulates antiviral specificity and prevents autoimmunity by controlling filament stability and downstream signaling, offering a mechanistic molecular explanation for disease pathogenesis.

title: Establishing the molecular basis for MDA5 mutation-linked autoimmunity.

abstract: Engineering autologous T cells for adoptive therapies has revolutionized cancer treatment, yet limited persistence remains a major barrier to robust clinical responses and durable disease control. Although costimulation with 4-1BB markedly improves CAR-T-cell persistence, no comparably effective approach has been identified to enhance persistence in T-cell therapies that rely on native TCR signaling, including conventional TCR-T cells and synthetic T-cell receptor and antigen receptor (STAR) T cells. To identify intrinsic persistence regulators in a TCR-based context, we performed an in vivo CRISPR activation screen in STAR-T cells and identified the noncanonical NF-κB axis, with RELB as the top hit. Direct RELB overexpression, however, exhibited dose-dependent cytotoxicity, motivating a translational alternative: overexpression of p52, the ncNF-κB transcription partner of RELB. Under prolonged antigen exposure, p52 overexpression sustained proliferation, preserved effector functions, and increased the intratumoral trafficking potential, particularly in CD8⁺ T cells, thereby yielding superior tumor control. Mechanistically, transcriptomic profiling revealed coordinated upregulation of cell cycle programs and chemokine receptors, along with downregulation of apoptosis and exhaustion-associated modules. Moreover, p52 overexpression restored RELB nuclear translocation in the context of PD-1/PD-L1 engagement, indicating partial resistance to checkpoint-mediated suppression and sustained ncNF-κB activity in PD-L1hi immunosuppressive environments. Collectively, our findings identify p52 as an antigen-dependent enhancer of ncNF-κB, conferring durable persistence and checkpoint resilience on TCR-based T cells and providing a feasible strategy to improve therapeutic effects in solid tumors.

title: How lipid nanoparticles evolved from models of biological membranes to systems that enable RNA therapeutics.

abstract: mRNA capping is a co-transcriptional, nuclear process in eukaryotes that adds a cap onto the 5' end of RNA to confer stability, efficient translation, and nuclear export. Viruses have evolved diverse strategies by mimicking or subverting host pathways to install an mRNA cap for efficient gene expression and evasion of the host innate immune response. The conventional mRNA capping pathway, employed by many RNA and DNA viruses, is mediated by dedicated RNA 5'-triphosphatase, guanylyltransferase, and methyltransferase enzymes. In contrast, many RNA viruses utilize unconventional capping mechanisms that diverge from the canonical pathway, offering unique opportunities to develop virus family-specific antiviral therapeutics. Among negative-sense RNA viruses, members of the order Mononegavirales harbor a unique capping domain, polyribonucleotidyltransferase (PRNTase), embedded within the viral RdRp large (L) protein. Unlike the conventional guanylyltransferase-mediated mechanism, PRNTase catalyzes mRNA capping through the formation of a covalent L-pRNA intermediate rather than the canonical GMP-enzyme intermediate. The HR motif in PRNTase, involved in covalent linking to mRNA, is highly conserved in non-segmented negative-strand RNA viruses. This review focuses on structural and functional insights into Mononegavirales capping, highlighting the conserved motifs and domain architecture that make it a promising therapeutic target.

title: Revisiting mRNA capping in Mononegavirales: a promising, yet underexplored antiviral target.

abstract: Patient-derived tumor organoids (PDOs) closely preserve the cellular heterogeneity, histopathology, and molecular features of the original tumors, making them powerful preclinical models. Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) are an emerging class of precision medicines that modulate gene expression at the RNA level with high target specificity, yet their application in organoid systems remains underexplored. Here, we adapted previously described protocols to establish a biobank of prostate cancer (PC) PDOs, achieving a high initial growth success rate (>90%). Histological and molecular analyses confirmed the preservation of key tumor features. Using these models, we assessed several ASOs, with particular emphasis on OGX-427 (Apatorsen), an ASO targeting heat shock protein 27 (HSP27) that has been evaluated in phase I/II clinical trials. While OGX-427 effectively suppressed HSP27 expression and inhibited cell growth in 2D cultures, its efficacy was markedly limited in 3D organoids, likely due to extracellular matrix and structural barriers. Removing Matrigel and applying single-cell transfection overcame these barriers, achieving efficient ASO uptake, significant target protein downregulation, and robust, dose-dependent inhibition of organoid growth. These findings underscore the utility of PDOs for evaluating ASO-based therapies and their potential to accelerate precision oncology strategies for PC and other malignancies.

title: Prostate Cancer Patient-Derived Organoids (PDOs) as Functional Avatars for Antisense Oligonucleotide (ASO)-Based Personalized Therapy.

abstract: Pulmonary metastasis remains a lethal challenge, necessitating potent mRNA vaccines to establish proactive immune surveillance. Although lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are the gold standard for delivery mRNA, the "PEG dilemma"-comprising immunogenicity and poor cellular engagement-critically limits their efficacy. Here, we developed a biocompatibility, PEG-free mRNA platform (SG-LNP) co-modified with sialic acid-dimyristoyl-glycerol (SA-DMG) and monosialotetrahexosylganglioside (GM1), enabling a customizable tissue-targeting delivery pathway. This platform leverages the SA-Siglec axis to target antigen-presenting cells (APCs), markedly enhancing APCs uptake and facilitating endosomal escape. Upon pulmonary inhalation, the vaccine directly targets pulmonary APCs, shortening immunological pathways and enabling in situ priming of multiple immune effector cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, natural killer cells, and T cells). Following intravenous administration, it selectively targets splenic APCs to orchestrate a systemic immune surveillance network. Furthermore, leveraging this vaccine platform with tunable delivery routes, we investigated the contributions of local and systemic immune toward the prevention of tumor lung metastasis. We found that inhaled SG-LNP elicit robust local immune activation, leading to markedly reduced melanoma infiltration in the lungs relative to conventional PEG-modified LNPs. Notably, systemic administration of SG-LNP drives more extensive expansion of circulating antigen-specific T cells and natural killer cells (NKs). This systemic mobilization effectively intercepts circulating tumor cells before pulmonary colonization, achieving complete prevention of pulmonary metastasis with 100% protective efficacy. Our findings demonstrate that systemic coordination outperforms localized activation in prophylactic of organ-specific metastasis, providing a strategic blueprint for the design and administration of next-generation PEG-free mRNA vaccines.

title: Dual-glycolipid engineered vaccine platform empowers delivery route customization to intercept tumor lung metastasis.

abstract: KRASG12D/TP53R175H mutations are hallmarks of malignant tumor progression and are associated with lymph node (LN) metastasis in solid tumor. Nevertheless, the mechanisms underlying KRASG12D/TP53R175H co-mutation-mediated LN metastasis remain unclear. Herein, we developed KRASG12D/TP53R175H mutation-related orthotopic xenograft models and demonstrated that KRASG12D/TP53R175H co-mutation promotes the lymphangiogenesis and LN metastasis. FUS is identified by next generation sequencing to be upregulated in tumor tissues harbouring KRASG12D/TP53R175H co-mutation across multi-center cohorts, wherein KRASG12D-mediated phosphorylation of TP53R175H promotes FUS transcriptional activation. Functionally, FUS-mediated extracellular vesicle (EV) promotes lymphangiogenesis and LN metastasis in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, upon KRASG12D/TP53R175H co ‑ mutation, FUS regulated circSCARNA10 biosynthesis and promotes EVs secretion by stabilizing RAB3B mRNA, leading to VEGFR3 transcription in lymphatic endothelial cells to trigger lymphangiogenesis and LN metastasis. Blockade of FUS inhibits LN metastasis in KrasG12D/+Trp53R172H/+Pdx-1-Cre (KPC) mice model. Clinically, detecting circSCARNA10 in serum-EVs exhibited higher diagnostic efficiency compared with traditional biomarkers, carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19-9) in distinguishing LN metastasis. Collectively, we highlight the precise mechanisms by which KRASG12D/TP53R175H co-mutation mediates EV secretion to trigger LN metastasis, providing a potential therapeutic target for KRASG12D/TP53R175H co-mutation - driven LN metastasis.

abstract: Quality control of lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) is central to development of mRNA therapeutics, yet ensemble measurements obscure critical heterogeneity in particle morphology and mRNA cargo loading. Here we introduce PINPOINT (Profiling Individual Nanoparticles with Precise Observation of INternalized Therapeutics), a single-particle nanoscopy platform for non-destructive, multiparametric profiling of preformulated LNP samples. Super-resolution imaging with Nile Red resolves size and morphology, while an optimized permeabilization strategy provides selective access to encapsulated mRNA without compromising LNP integrity. Single-particle fluorescence measurements, including RiboGreen and sequence-specific probes, enable quantification and validation of mRNA loading and identity. Comparative analyses of bare and encapsulated mRNA reveal kinetic and structural features, exposing heterogeneity masked by bulk assays. By integrating structural and molecular readouts at the single-particle level, PINPOINT establishes a quantitative framework for assessing of LNP composition and payload distribution, offering actionable insights for improving batch consistency and guiding the rational design of next-generation mRNA delivery systems.

abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is driven by cancer stemness and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, which collectively contribute to therapeutic resistance. While the RNA-binding protein HNRNPC has been implicated in tumor progression, it has primarily been characterized as a downstream effector, and its autonomous regulatory functions, particularly in governing cancer stemness, remain entirely unexplored. Through multi-omics analyses of HCC cohorts, we identified HNRNPC as a pivotal driver of a high-risk molecular subtype. Mechanistically, HNRNPC expression was transcriptionally activated via WDR5/KMT2A complex-mediated deposition of H3K4me3 at its promoter. Functionally, HNRNPC was essential for maintaining cancer stemness, promoting tumor growth and metastasis, and conferring oxaliplatin resistance. Notably, depletion of HNRNPC reprogrammed the immunosuppressive microenvironment by enhancing CD8+ T cell infiltration, reducing T cell exhaustion, and polarizing macrophages toward an M1-like anti-tumor phenotype. At the molecular level, HNRNPC bound to the m6A-modified 3'UTR of CD24 mRNA in an RNP2 motif-dependent manner, thereby enhancing its stability and elevating CD24 protein expression. Therapeutically, we developed a novel lipid nanoparticle (LNP) encapsulating siRNA against HNRNPC. Systemically administered AP-EG-si potently suppressed tumor growth, attenuated stemness, and synergized with anti-PD-L1 therapy to enhance anti-tumor immunity. Our findings thus unveil the H3K4me3-HNRNPC-CD24 axis as a central epigenetic and post-transcriptional regulatory pathway that coordinately drives HCC stemness and immune evasion, nominating HNRNPC-targeted nanotherapy as a promising strategy for advanced HCC.

abstract: Neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson's Disease (PD), Alzheimer's Disease (AD), Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), and Huntington's Disease (HD) are characterized by progressive neuronal degeneration and severe therapeutic limitations due to the Blood-Brain Barrier (BBB). Recent advances in nanotechnology have enabled the development of nanoscale drug delivery systems capable of improving BBB penetration and enhancing therapeutic efficacy. This review discusses recent progress in Lipid Nanoparticles (LNPs), polymeric nanoparticles, exosomes, magnetic nanoparticles, gold nanoparticles, graphene quantum dots, and RNAloaded nanocarriers for brain-targeted delivery. Special emphasis is placed on receptor-mediated transcytosis, intranasal delivery, magnetic targeting, and ionizable lipid nanoparticle systems for nucleic acid delivery. Recent nanoformulations including curcumin-loaded nanoparticles, siRNA- loaded lipid nanoparticles, dopamine-loaded liposomes, and lactoferrin-functionalized polymeric nanoparticles are critically compared based on BBB penetration, therapeutic efficacy, toxicity, and translational potential. Furthermore, current clinical challenges including nanotoxicity, pharmacokinetics, large-scale manufacturing, and regulatory barriers are discussed. Nanotechnology- based therapeutics represent a promising strategy for improving diagnosis and treatment of neurodegenerative disorders and may facilitate the future development of precision nanomedicine.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Avian influenza viruses (AIVs), particularly highly pathogenic H5 and H7 viruses, pose major threats to poultry production, food security, international trade, and public health. Vaccination is an important component of AIV control; however, antigenic evolution, incomplete reduction of viral shedding, and challenges associated with large-scale poultry vaccination limit its effectiveness. In addition to conventional vaccines, recombinant and nucleic-acid platforms have emerged in response to rapidly evolving AIVs.
METHODS: Relevant literature on inactivated, live attenuated, recombinant subunit, viral-vector, DNA, mRNA, and virus-like particle vaccines was evaluated. Immune responses, protection, antigenic breadth, viral shedding, delivery, manufacturing, field applicability, and regulatory considerations were analyzed.
RESULTS: Inactivated vaccines are well-established, safe, scalable, and cost-effective but provide limited cellular and mucosal immunity and require antigenic matching. Live attenuated vaccines can induce broader immunity and facilitate mass vaccination but present biosafety, reassortment, and genetic-stability concerns. Next-generation platforms provide greater antigenic flexibility and opportunities for broader protection. Viral-vector vaccines can induce both humoral and cellular immunity, while recombinant subunit, DNA, mRNA, and VLP vaccines offer rapid redesign and multivalent formulations. However, challenges remain regarding delivery, stability, manufacturing, durability, and field validation.
CONCLUSIONS: No single platform currently meets all requirements for sustainable AIV control. Future strategies should emphasize conserved or mosaic antigens, durable and mucosal immunity, rapid vaccine updating, DIVA compatibility, and scalable delivery. Combining conventional and emerging platforms through prime-boost or multi-platform strategies may provide more flexible and effective control.

abstract: Thioredoxin-interacting protein (TXNIP) is a multifunctional regulatory protein of the α-arrestin family that acts as a redox sensor, an energy-responsive molecule, and a transcription-associated regulator. TXNIP has emerged as a key regulator of skeletal muscle homeostasis and has been implicated in the pathogenesis of multiple muscle disorders. Skeletal muscle is a principal site of systemic glucose disposal, accounting for more than 70% of insulin-stimulated glucose uptake in the human body. TXNIP has been implicated in sarcopenia, obesity-related insulin resistance, limb ischemia-induced muscle injury, disuse muscle atrophy, and hereditary muscular dystrophy through multiple mechanisms, including glutathione metabolic regulation, ferroptosis, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, impaired GLUT4 membrane translocation, and altered mitochondrial substrate oxidation. Recent advances in gene editing, single-cell sequencing, metabolomics, and human clinical research have enabled a more detailed characterization of TXNIP-related molecular mechanisms in skeletal muscle. This review provides a systematic synthesis of recent evidence on TXNIP in skeletal muscle, organized around seven themes: its molecular characteristics, expression and regulatory patterns in skeletal muscle, physiological functions, disease-specific pathogenic mechanisms, intervention-related regulatory networks, current limitations, and future perspectives. This review aims to provide a mechanistic rationale for targeting TXNIP as a potential strategy for the prevention and treatment of skeletal muscle-related diseases.

abstract: Autosomal dominant loss-of-function variants in the gene MYBPC3 are, collectively, the most common genetic cause of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) and are a prototype of haploinsufficient human disease. Typical for haploinsufficiency-associated genes, hundreds of unique loss-of-function pathogenic variants have been reported for MYBPC3 - therapeutic gene editing to correct each of these variants poses major regulatory and logistical hurdles. Upregulating wild-type allele expression could offer a generalizable therapeutic strategy, but the capacity to modulate native MYBPC3 transcription is unknown. Here, we present a variant-agnostic approach to rescue haploinsufficiency by mapping and rationally redesigning the MYBPC3 promoter. Using massively parallel reporter assays (MPRAs) in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes, we performed saturation mutagenesis of the MYBPC3 promoter at single base-pair resolution. This defined a new class of clinically relevant noncoding loss-of-function variants while revealing essential cis-regulatory grammar anchored by key transcription factor binding sites (TFBSs). Furthermore, by systematically screening thousands of variant combinations, modular promoter elements, and heterologous TFBS insertions, we identified synergistic sequence edits that drive robust increases in MYBPC3 expression. Together, our findings improve the clinical interpretation of noncoding variants and establish a scalable blueprint for promoter editing to treat MYBPC3 -associated HCM and other haploinsufficient diseases.

abstract: Global aquaculture faces an escalating disease and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) crisis, exacerbated by climate-driven physiochemical shifts and intensive farming practices. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and structural biology, spearheaded by AlphaFold, represents a paradigm shift in aquatic pharmacology, transitioning the field from empirical trial-and-error to rational in silico design. This review critically evaluates the application of AI-driven tools in aquaculture drug discovery and vaccine development. We examine the evolution of AlphaFold in predicting complex host-pathogen interactions and facilitating de novo drug design. Concurrently, we highlight critical limitations stemming from the reliance on multiple sequence alignment (MSA) depth rather than mere PDB taxonomic composition, the unreliability of direct molecular docking due to apo conformations, and the dynamic nature of psychrophilic adaptations in aquatic environments. Furthermore, we assess next-generation structural vaccinology, including reverse vaccinology and pre-fusion antigen stabilization, alongside the integration of nanomaterial-based delivery systems to overcome aquatic pharmacokinetic barriers. The synergy of AI with CRISPR/Cas technologies and multimodal large language models (MM-LLMs) for disease management is also explored. Despite unprecedented computational capabilities, significant bottlenecks remain, including a severe lack of species-specific omics data, the indispensability of in vivo wet-lab validation, and lagging regulatory frameworks. Ultimately, realizing the potential of precision aquatic medicine requires developing aquaculture-specific databases, addressing the ecological risks of open-water deployment, and democratizing these technologies for small-scale farmers to ensure sustainable, equitable, and resilient global aquaculture.

abstract: Nucleic-acid biomarkers play pivotal roles in disease diagnosis, therapeutic monitoring, and precision medicine, creating an urgent demand for analytical platforms combining high sensitivity, molecular specificity, and rapid detection. Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) integrated with aptamers, short single-stranded DNA or RNA oligonucleotides, has attracted considerable attention by coupling programmable molecular recognition with ultrasensitive plasmon-enhanced Raman detection. This review evaluates recent advances in aptamer-based SERS biosensors for nucleic-acid analysis, systematically examining sensing mechanisms, plasmonic substrate engineering, aptamer immobilization, signal-transduction pathways, and amplification approaches, including catalytic hairpin assembly, hybridization chain reaction, rolling circle amplification, and CRISPR-assisted systems. Recent developments in microfluidics, artificial intelligence-assisted spectral analysis, portable Raman instrumentation, and point-of-care platforms are assessed while distinguishing true aptamer-mediated sensing from conventional hybridization-based DNA detection. Rational hotspot engineering, deterministic nanogap architectures, and advanced amplification strategies have enabled detection from femtomolar to attomolar levels with improved selectivity, multiplexing, and reproducibility. Challenges including substrate variability, quantitative standardization, aptamer stability, biosafety, and clinical translation are discussed. Future directions toward standardized, intelligent, clinically deployable SERS platforms for next-generation molecular diagnostics and precision healthcare are proposed.

abstract: Alternative splicing is a key regulatory mechanism known to be altered upon viral infection. These alterations can arise both from direct viral interference with the splicing machinery and from cellular responses such as activation of innate immunity. Here, we investigated splicing changes shared between dengue virus (DENV) infection and interferon (IFN) treatment in cultured cells, the latter serving as a model for virus-independent innate immune activation. Among the common events, we identified an increased production of non-coding mRNA isoforms from the CLK1 gene, which gives rise to a kinase that phosphorylates splicing factors including SR proteins and spliceosomal components. Consistent with this finding, IFN treatment led to a reduction in CLK1 protein levels. Using stable cell lines with CRISPR/dCas9-mediated modulation of CLK1 expression, we found that silencing CLK1 enhanced the induction of immune response genes, while its over-expression attenuated it. Inhibition of CLK1 kinase activity with the pharmacological inhibitor TG003 further potentiated IFN-induced gene expression and reduced DENV replication. Altogether, these results identify CLK1 as a proviral negative regulator of IFN-stimulated gene expression and suggest that its inhibition could enhance antiviral defenses and become a target for therapeutic strategies.
